**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of O'Connor's opinion, joined by the same five Justices as Part II; six direct joins.

**Material application:** Underinclusion may reveal a failed justification, but every imperfect boundary is not invalid. Direct receipt places the treasury contribution under the candidate's control, a relation not established for every party use. Reported coordination does not certify the legality of all described arrangements, and ideological agreement is not itself coordination.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding does not validate unchallenged soft-money practices, classify every party expenditure, or let resources of a different association automatically answer a burden on the chosen one.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** FEC v. Akins, June 25, 1997, preserves actual transaction definitions, candidate connection, thresholds, and distinct exclusions and reporting provisos. Day v. Holahan retains its pooling, meaningful-association, nonprofit independent-spending protections, and unresolved responsive-financing rationale. Daggett's contribution and cumulative-burden rules remain bounded to their adopted grounds; public financing cannot cure an independent private restraint.

##### Independent constitutional protection of truthful contribution attribution

**Holding:** Congress may address truthful source attribution and evasion in the presented candidate-contribution transactions by prohibiting contributions in another's name, knowing permission to use one's name, and knowing acceptance of falsely attributed contributions. The constitutional objection to the alleged knowing reimbursement scheme fails independently of the corporate-source rule; regulatory differences elsewhere create no entitlement to substitute a false donor.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part IV of O'Connor's opinion, unanimous on this bounded constitutional answer.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 441f's first clause lacks an express knowledge word, while its second and third clauses contain one. That textual difference is neither a strict-criminal-liability holding nor construction of the enforcement provision's elements. Innocent-error applications remain unadjudicated. A supported reasonable probability of threats, harassment, or reprisals retains its own disclosure protection and possible nondisclosure remedy, without authorizing false naming; no such showing is established here. No general identification rule for all political association follows.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Both corporate constitutional answers are affirmed 6-3 and the independent false-source answer 9-0. The pending criminal process must independently determine corporate source where relevant, true attribution, applicable knowledge, and every other element and defense. Allegations establish no guilt, completed exchange, count sufficiency, penalty, or charge under every clause. No acquittal, replacement ceiling, refund, damages, severability remedy, or order governing unchallenged party financing follows.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Buckley supports contribution information and enforcement interests without approving every restriction. McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission, April 19, 1995, protects truthful anonymous advocacy while preserving distinct candidate-finance attribution and tailored impersonation controls; supported nondisclosure protection does not authorize a false name.

**Material application:** The presented holdings retain the following statutory scope and qualifications.

The direct-treasury holding concerns the presented business-corporation-to-federal-candidate class. Section 441b(a) covers national-bank and congressionally organized corporate contributions or expenditures in elections for any political office, including candidate-selection primaries, conventions, and caucuses. For corporations generally and labor organizations, it covers elections for presidential and vice-presidential electors, Senators, Representatives, Delegates, and Resident Commissioners, and the corresponding nomination processes. It separately prohibits knowing acceptance or receipt by candidates, political committees, or other persons, and consent to prohibited organizational contributions or expenditures by corporate or bank officers or directors and labor-organization officers. A labor organization includes an organization, agency, employee committee, or plan with employee participation and at least a partial purpose of dealing with employers over grievances, labor disputes, wages, pay rates, hours, or working conditions. These distinct classes receive no new independent holdings merely because they share the section; independent expenditures and press activity remain outside this decision.

Section 441b(b)(2) reaches direct or indirect payments, distributions, loans, advances, deposits, gifts, services, and value to candidates, campaign committees, political parties, or organizations in connection with covered elections. It excepts ordinary-course national or State bank loans complying with applicable banking law and regulations. Three separate exclusions protect corporate communications on any subject to stockholders, executive or administrative personnel, and their families, or labor communications to members and families; nonpartisan registration and get-out-the-vote activity directed to the corresponding groups; and establishment, administration, and solicitation for separate segregated political funds by corporations, labor organizations, membership organizations, cooperatives, and nonstock corporations. The distinct membership-communication exclusion and reporting proviso in §431, preserved in Akins, are not substituted for these provisions.

The political fund cannot use value obtained by physical force, job discrimination, financial reprisal or threats; payments required for labor-organization membership or employment; or commercial transactions. Any person soliciting an employee must disclose, at the time of solicitation, the fund's political purpose and the employee's right to refuse without reprisal. Corporate support for establishment, administration, and solicitation does not authorize treasury money as the fund's candidate-contribution money.

Ordinary corporate solicitation reaches stockholders, executive or administrative personnel, and their families; ordinary labor solicitation reaches members and their families. Corporations, labor organizations, and their funds may also make two written solicitations per calendar year to corporate stockholders, executive or administrative personnel, employees, and their families, mailed to residences and designed to conceal from the solicitor who gives $50 or less and who gives nothing. Additional routes preserve member solicitation by membership organizations, cooperatives, nonstock corporations, and their funds, and trade-association or trade-association-fund solicitation with a member corporation's separate, specific approval, limited to one association per corporation per calendar year. That trade-association route reaches the approving member corporation's stockholders, executive or administrative personnel, and their families.

Lawful methods of soliciting or facilitating voluntary fund contributions available to corporations for stockholders and executive or administrative personnel must also be available to labor organizations for members. A corporation using those methods, including its subsidiaries, branches, divisions, and affiliates, must provide them on written request to a labor organization representing members working for those entities at reimbursement of expenses only. Executive or administrative personnel must be salaried rather than hourly and have policymaking, managerial, professional, or supervisory responsibility. These statutory routes establish no finding that the particular companies possess a successful fund, sufficient donor pool, or practical resources.

Section 441f contains no internal blanket exception. The actual contribution definition, true source, attributable reporting, knowledge and enforcement requirements, and supported associational protections retain their separate work. None of the indictment allegations supplies a completed exchange, corrupt intent, knowledge, or actual influence finding.

For section 437h eligibility, substantiality, and the review route, see this case, Third Circuit No. 99-3875, December 12, 2000, under Federal Courts, Certified campaign-finance constitutional questions.

### Official congressional ballot policy penalties

#### Cook v. Gralike, 531 U.S. 510

**Docket or dockets:** No. 99-929.
**Decided:** February 28, 2001.

##### Whether congressional ballots may penalize refusal of a state-selected legislative position

**Holding:** The Elections Clause does not authorize a State to use its official congressional ballot to disadvantage candidates because they refuse a prescribed position or pledge concerning future federal legislation. Adverse labels triggered by noncompliance with the State's selected policy exceed election-manner authority even when the candidate remains eligible and the name stays on the ballot.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's Court opinion has seven supporters for the constitutional source rule: Stevens, Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Those seven and Thomas support the label application; Thomas accepts the parties' source premise only for this litigation. O'Connor agrees in judgment on a separate speech ground and supplies no structural rationale join.

**Material application:** Thornton supplies the source principle that authority over congressional balloting rests on constitutional delegation, not a reserved power over previously nonexistent federal offices. These labels impose an official electoral disadvantage for rejecting a policy program even though eligibility and ballot access remain. Quantified proof of lost votes is unnecessary.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The labels fail even assuming the enactment may exercise the manner power; the referendum/legislature question is therefore not decided. No Court speech holding, general public-forum theory, prohibition on private advocacy or genuinely nonbinding requests, or restriction on unrelated neutral information is adopted.

##### Whether affirmance preserves the actual sections 15-19 injunction

**Holding:** The judgment preserving the injunction against Article VIII sections 15–19 is affirmed. Because the State defended the enactment in its entirety and sought no alternative severance if that defense failed, the Court leaves the reviewed decree undisturbed rather than substituting a new label-only decree or independently deciding the validity of every nonbinding instruction.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer directly adopt the full decree account. Stone-Zsela joins the label relief and concurs only in the residual sections 15-16 judgment. The disposition is unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 19 label review and its clear-and-convincing burden are distinct from section 20 automatic repeal, section 21 forum and section 22 severability. The severability clause does not by itself select new relief. Affirmance makes no separate constitutional holding about every nonbinding instruction and creates no Missouri severability rule.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The injunction against sections 15-19 remains enforceable at its existing scope. The State defended the whole enactment without seeking alternative severance here; no replacement label-only decree or rewrite is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton: extends the distinction between genuine election procedure and substantive candidate disadvantage to adverse policy-compliance labels; its exclusive-qualifications and national-office source holdings remain in force.
- Libertarian Party of Illinois v. Rednour: distinguishes genuine support and nomination procedure from the official political penalty here; ordinary access regulation retains its separate constitutional review.
- Anderson v. Martin: applies the official ballot's capacity to impose a candidate disadvantage; the Court's sufficient rule here rests on the Elections Clause.
- Burdick v. Takushi: preserves calibrated review of actual electoral burdens and legitimate administration; it supplies no authority for official favoritism among substantive political positions.

### Presidential-election timing and fairness

#### Bush v. Palm Beach County Canvassing Board, 531 U.S. 70

**Docket or dockets:** No. 00-836.
**Decided:** December 4, 2000.

##### Section 5's conditional benefit and the distinct due-process inquiry

**Holding:** Then-operative 3 U.S.C. section 5 grants conclusive treatment in the federal count to a qualifying final determination under pre-election state law made at least six days before the electors meet; it does not itself forbid all later counting. Due process separately distinguishes authoritative construction of ambiguity from fundamental unfairness; post-vote interpretation or conflicting advice alone establishes no violation, and the submitted fairness issue returns on the clarified state-law premises.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II's timing proposition has all nine Justices' joins. Part III's due-process rationale is supported by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer; Stone-Zsela joins only that component's remand disposition.

**Material application:** December 12 is the six-day date for the December 18 meeting, without itself becoming an absolute state-law termination date. Actual official guidance, dissemination, inducement, reliance, and voting circumstances matter to fairness without constituting a new rigid checklist. Conflicting post-election advice does not establish a pre-election assurance or detrimental reliance.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court neither finds qualification for or loss of section 5's benefit nor resolves a due-process violation. Whether a clear rule was displaced instead of an ambiguity construed depends partly on the state-law clarification. No general prohibition on state constitutional interpretation is adopted.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The federal components return within the defined vacatur-and-clarification disposition; no counting stay or terminal federal date is created.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Foster v. Love retains its congressional final-selection rule and express presidential-timing reservation. Citizens for a Constitutional Convention v. Yoshina, January 21, 1999, supplies the fundamental-fairness distinction and prevents automatic invalidation for a neutral interpretation differing from earlier advice.

For finality, clarification scope, and the operative remedy, see this case, No. 00-836, December 4, 2000, under Federal Courts, Review of state judgments and clarification remands.

### Statewide judicial vote determinations

#### Bush v. Gore

**Docket or dockets:** No. 00-949; review of Florida Supreme Court No. SC00-2431.
**Decided:** December 12, 2000.

##### Equal treatment of materially comparable ballots in a statewide judicial determination

**Holding:** A statewide judicial determination combining recovered votes with further examination cannot apply materially arbitrary operative criteria to legally comparable ballots. The supervising court must provide sufficiently definite, consistent, reviewable applications of the existing legal-vote standard, while allowing relevant physical-evidence differences and ordinary variations that do not produce material inequality.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, and Breyer; seven Justices. Stevens and Ginsburg reject liability in this decree.

**Material application:** Supported testimony identifies conflicting Miami-Dade thresholds for dimples, separation, light, and other indications, and changing Palm Beach whole-ballot approaches without established consistent reconsideration of all affected earlier rulings. Combining those recovered votes and further examination under a general intent direction leaves material operative conflicts unresolved. Official honesty and a valid general rule do not themselves cure that defect.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Mere disagreement, equipment differences, or an unclear mark establishes no violation. Bad faith, proof of a changed winner, a complete matched-ballot study, duplicate votes, and recovery of votes from every overvote are not required findings. The rule is not limited to these candidates or this election and creates no national physical-mark code.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections and Reynolds v. Sims supply equal participation and voting-weight principles for actual crediting criteria. Burdick v. Takushi, June 8, 1992, preserves reasonable neutral administration but not material unequal treatment. Shaw v. Reno, June 28, 1993, retains its rejection of territorial design alone as deprivation; actual unequal ballot valuation is distinct.

##### The separate due-process objection to authoritative interpretation

**Holding:** A neutral judicial construction of ambiguity does not become fundamentally unfair solely because it differs from asserted practice or advisory interpretation. A supported inducement or frustrated-choice claim requires consideration of the actual directions, dissemination, reliance, and voting circumstances; this record supplies no independent due-process basis for reversal.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part IV of Souter's opinion, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; eight Justices. Stone-Zsela agrees only in the component disposition.

**Material application:** The pre-existing contest and voter-intent provisions and the state court's statutory explanation prevent an inference of unfairness from interpretation alone. No established pre-election assurance, dissemination, or detrimental reliance supports the distinct deprivation asserted here.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Absence of those facts establishes neither litigant default nor misleading conduct. Deliberate official misdirection, pervasive frustration of effective choice, and supported reliance claims remain distinct. Equal-treatment liability requires no official-inducement finding.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Citizens for a Constitutional Convention v. Yoshina, January 21, 1999, supplies the actual unfairness inquiry. Palm Beach, December 4, 2000, preserved that inquiry apart from Article II rather than equating the two.

##### Section 5's conditional federal benefit and the elector meeting

**Holding:** Under then-operative 3 U.S.C. section 5, a final determination of an elector-appointment controversy through procedures established in state law before election day receives conclusive federal-count treatment if made pursuant to that law at least six days before the electors meet. December 12 is the qualifying date for the December 18 meeting, but section 5 alone forbids no later counting, independently applicable state limits remain binding, and section 7's meeting date remains fixed.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part V-A of Souter's opinion, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No qualification for or forfeiture of the federal benefit, completed count, feasibility, impossibility, or comprehensive rule for competing electoral submissions is decided from the calendar alone.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Palm Beach preserves the distinction between conditional federal benefit and state-law deadline. Foster v. Love, December 2, 1997, concerns premature final congressional selection and supplies no presidential counting cutoff.

##### Authoritative resolution of the precise state-law termination consequence

**Holding:** The December 11 state clarification does not require this Court to impose categorical December 12 termination of every corrective contest proceeding. The state judiciary must authoritatively determine the precise consequence of its governing timing law for lawful and feasible correction; this directive permits neither disregard of a binding state limit nor completion until December 18 as of right.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part V-C has five direct joins: Souter, Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Stevens and Ginsburg continue to oppose vacatur; their timing joins are not votes for that judgment. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas construe state law to require December 12 finality.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The unresolved consequence concerns state law, not section 5's settled character. No extension, postponed elector meeting, or presumed winner is supplied.

##### Defined correction of the established unequal-treatment defect

**Holding:** The affected inclusion and examination directions must be vacated and returned immediately for consistent, reviewable application of existing state law, including affected earlier additions when necessary to cure material inequality. Correction requires lawful authority, accurate figures, an adequate process, and actual feasibility; the defect does not itself terminate the entire contest or award electoral votes.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part V-B of Souter's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Breyer; five direct joins. Scalia and Thomas choose independent Article II reversal, with equality correction only as a conditional alternative. Stevens and Ginsburg would affirm. The operative judgment is therefore 5-2-2, not seven unconditional votes for the same remand.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The mandate issues immediately. The state court must reconcile affected earlier inclusions and further examination, resolve Palm Beach's disputed net 215/176 figure before lawful inclusion, distinguish the Miami-Dade partial return from the unexamined undervote pool, and permit meaningful objection and review. Supported claims about comparable excluded legal votes require an answer; neither universal overvote examination nor repetition of a proper examination absent material inconsistency follows. A vote is not discarded merely because relevant physical evidence differs.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The rejected Nassau adjustment and claim to reexamine approximately 3,300 previously examined Palm Beach ballots remain undisturbed limits, without new federal merits adjudication. Neither completed implementation nor present impossibility is established, and absence of impossibility proves no feasible completion. The state judiciary must determine authority, binding timing, and practical feasibility. The Court retains no counting supervision, imposes no separate stay, decides no unpresented stay request, fixes no tally, and awards no candidate Florida's electoral votes.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Palm Beach supplies bounded correction respectful of lawful state administration, without a recount stay or candidate result. The equality rule requires correction of operative criteria, not a presumed electoral outcome.

For the Article II holding, see this case, No. 00-949, December 12, 2000, under Constitutional Structure, Legislative direction of presidential-elector appointment. For the section 1257 threshold, see Federal Courts, Immediate review of state decrees under Cox.


### Racial predominance and a cognizable districting injury

#### Easley v. Cromartie / Smallwood v. Cromartie, 532 U.S. 234

**Docket or dockets:** Nos. 99-1864 and 99-1865.
**Decided:** April 18, 2001.
**Companion or consolidated matters:** The State and intervenors challenge the same three-judge judgment; both receive the same mandate.

##### Whether a completed racial-predominance finding establishes a districting injury

**Holding:** A common territorial district is not invalid solely because racial considerations predominated and ordinary districting criteria were subordinated. Relief requires an actually presented and preserved exclusion, intentional dilution, materially unequal participation, inferior civic membership or other independent deprivation, assessed under that claim's own elements, burdens and justification rules; without such a claim, judgment must be entered for defendants on the insufficient design-only theory.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Breyer: five Justices. All nine support immediate vacatur, but O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas do not join the controlling rule or remand limitation.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Shape, racial and political correlation, communications, maps and electoral experience remain usable evidence, not automatic injury. No universal statistical model or alternative-map requirement is imposed; the actual claim's requirements remain. A partisan explanation cannot defeat a proved wrong, and unequal treatment need not produce a second governmental act, electoral defeat or financial loss. Actual preservation and proof of an independent claim are not found.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Vacate both judgments and dependent relief and remand only for actually presented, preserved independent claims under ordinary procedure. The mandate creates no new claim, final map-validity determination, replacement plan, election change, quota or automatic discovery entitlement.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Shaw v. Reno, Johnson v. Miller and Bush v. Vera retain the territorial-design boundary and independent-injury protections. Hunt v. Cromartie's prior mandate is enforced; a predominance-only trial does not satisfy it. Adarand governs justification for an actual covered racial allocation, not creation of a missing cause of action. Ordinary factual deference cannot transform legally insufficient predominance into injury.

### Population bases for representative districts

#### Chen v. City of Houston

**Docket or dockets:** Fifth Circuit No. 98-20440; judgment below, 206 F.3d 502.
**Decided:** May 21, 2001.

##### Whether unequal citizen voting-age populations forbid municipal districts based on total resident population

**Holding:** A municipality may use total resident population for ordinary representative council districts even when citizen voting-age populations materially differ. Representing all residents is a permissible constitutional objective; differences in eligible electorates alone do not compel another denominator or a new election.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's unanimous opinion of the Court.

**Material application:** Houston's 8.63-percent maximum total-population deviation supplies neither a requirement to substitute citizen voting-age population nor immunity from every constitutional claim. Deviation is measured after choosing the legally permissible population base; preclearance does not decide the constitutional question.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The ruling does not require total population universally, approve another proposed denominator, or decide the separate racial-gerrymandering claim. Intentional exclusion and independently established dilution remain distinct; no demographic or alternative-map finding is made.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The Fifth Circuit is affirmed on the accepted population-base claim; no redistricting, demographic hearing or election relief is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Reynolds v. Sims and Avery v. Midland County supply districting equality without compelling an eligible-voter denominator. Burns v. Richardson preserves permissible population choices. Voinovich v. Quilter governs deviations within the legally relevant measure, without categorical protection below ten percent. United States Department of Commerce v. Montana preserves review despite legislative choice, without transferring its interstate-allocation holding to intrastate districts. Easley v. Cromartie and Smallwood v. Cromartie remain distinct racial-districting authority.



### Actually coordinated political-party expenditures

#### FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee

**Docket or dockets:** No. 00-191.
**Decided:** June 25, 2001.

##### Whether the presented Senate party-spending ceiling survives the categorical facial challenge

**Holding:** Congress may limit expenditures actually coordinated with a federal candidate when the government demonstrates an objectively grounded risk of circumvention of valid candidate-contribution limits and a restriction closely drawn to that risk while preserving meaningful party association and effective advocacy. On this developed record, the presented Senate-election party ceiling satisfies that standard against the categorical facial challenge; party identity, policy agreement, endorsement or ordinary affiliation alone establishes neither coordination nor corruption.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Ginsburg; six direct votes for both holdings and their qualifications.

**Material application:** The developed evidence of donor understandings, fundraising credits and allocation arrangements establishes a practical candidate-limit circumvention channel without a completed bribe or a finding that every tally is unlawful. Formal earmark enforcement alone does not reach tacit understandings and general-treasury allocation. The Court weighs coordination's real association costs and the substantial coordinated activity still permitted; unlimited independent spending is not alone an answer to those burdens.

Section 441a(a)(7)(B)(i) requires actual cooperation, consultation or concert with, or a request or suggestion from, a candidate, an authorized political committee or an agent. Section (a)(7)(B)(ii) separately addresses financing dissemination, distribution or republication of candidate-prepared campaign material; it is not the same predicate. Section (a)(8) attributes a contribution directed through an intermediary or conduit to its original source and requires source-and-recipient reporting. The (a)(4) exception for transfers among national, State, district, local and subordinate committees of the same party applies to the limits in (a)(1) and (2); it supplies no categorical constitutional immunity for candidate-connected spending.

Section (d)(1) permits the identified national and State party committees, including subordinate State committees, to make general-election expenditures notwithstanding other contribution or expenditure limits, subject to (d)(2) and (3). Section (d)(3)(A)'s Senate and single-Representative-State allowance is the greater of two cents per voting-age resident or $20,000, increased under (c)'s annual price-index adjustment. Section (d)(3)(B)'s separate $10,000 indexed allowance concerns other House, Delegate and Resident Commissioner races. The present constitutional holding concerns the Senate counterclaim; it does not independently adjudicate those other categories or the presidential allowance, replace the statutory amounts, or erase ordinary contribution and genuine-conduit distinctions.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Ordinary access, equalization and opposition to campaign expense supply no independent justification. A particular jointly expressed communication may require distinct constitutional characterization; the facial record does not resolve that question or establish the extent needed for broader overbreadth relief. No materially different ceiling, unconnected spending, presidential allowance, other House category, all soft-money practice or universal empirical safe harbor is approved.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Buckley supplies the functional contribution/expenditure distinction. Colorado Republican v. FEC (June 26, 1996) retains its six-Justice protection of genuinely independent expression and actual candidate connection; this decision resolves its reserved facial coordinated-spending question. Russell, Shrink Missouri and Daggett require an objective government showing and close fit without a fixed dollar floor. Day preserves meaningful intermediary association and realistic conduit regulation. Mariani distinguishes direct candidate resources from different party arrangements and retains its separate false-source holding.

##### Whether rejection of the broader counterclaim alters the earlier independent-advertisement judgment

**Holding:** The Tenth Circuit's judgment sustaining facial invalidation of the presented coordinated-party expenditure ceiling is reversed, and the case is remanded for rejection of the party's categorical exemption claim and conforming proceedings. The earlier judgment protecting the genuinely independent advertisements remains effective; any remaining enforcement matter requires its own actual statutory predicates and lawful liability and remedial findings.

**Proposition-level authority:** Breyer's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Ginsburg; six direct votes for both holdings and their qualifications.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The accepted independence of the pre-nomination advertisements is not reopened. The party abandoned its earlier inseverability argument, which supplies neither a new holding nor a remedial instruction.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The facial invalidation is reversed and the case remanded for rejection of categorical party immunity and conforming proceedings. No specific transaction is newly found coordinated; no civil penalty, refund, damages, donor attribution, replacement ceiling or mandatory new trial is ordered.

### Independent Senate nomination deadlines

#### Wood v. Meadows

**Docket or dockets:** Fourth Circuit No. 99-1069; district court No. CA-94-47-D; judgment below, 207 F.3d 708. No Supreme Court docket is established.
**Decided:** June 11, 2001.

For the continuing-controversy holding in Wood v. Meadows, June 11, 2001, Fourth Circuit No. 99-1069, see Federal Courts — Recurring election controversies after the challenged election.

##### This accessible nomination system proportionately supports the June deadline

**Holding:** A State may close independent Senate nomination on its June primary date when the complete scheme affords a substantial practical petition period, reasonably attainable support requirements, multiple petition signing, retained primary participation and time after primary candidates file to organize independently, and when common nomination timing and orderly preparation proportionately justify the actual burden. Virginia's demonstrated system satisfies that standard; calling a restriction reasonable does not eliminate scrutiny of the relationship between burden and asserted interests.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter's complete opinion is supported by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer, including its author. Those seven direct joins control the application and affirmance.

**Material application:** The challenged election required 14,865 signatures, including 200 per district, with collection from January 1, multiple signing, retained primary participation and no prior disaffiliation. Primary candidates filed sixty days before the June deadline. Independents therefore had a meaningful organization period but could not await primary results. That lost opportunity was a real, nonsevere burden in the complete system. About thirty days were needed for processing, so verification alone did not justify all 150 days; common nomination timing and an orderly general-election campaign supplied additional proportional grounds.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Anderson's actual burden, precise interests and fit inquiry remains mandatory. Under Burdick, severe restrictions require compelling-interest narrow tailoring; reasonable nondiscriminatory restrictions permit proportionate important regulatory interests. Formal equality and primary-day coincidence supply no safe harbor. The Court requires neither the latest mechanically possible date nor an opportunity to await every later preference; materially different cumulative barriers require their own review.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The judgment sustaining Virginia's deadline is affirmed and prospective relief denied, while the lower court's categorical no-fit formulation is rejected. No replacement date, ballot placement or reopening of an election is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Anderson v. Celebrezze: applied as the actual burden, precise interest and fit inquiry; its earlier presidential deadline does not mechanically decide this Senate system.
- Burdick v. Takushi: applied without changing its calibrated scrutiny; its effective-route holding concerns ordinary nomination routes that close before voters can respond to the actual field, and this system leaves independents meaningful time to organize after primary candidates file, without any entitlement to every late candidacy.
- Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New Party: applied for genuine fit between a nomination burden and the State's precise interests, leaving orderly candidate-selection rules available; it remains neither pure rational-basis review nor permission to suppress competition.
- Norman v. Reed and Moore v. Ogilvie: applied to the continuing election controversy and meaningful access; support screening remains permissible within the actual electorate.
- Storer v. Brown: applied for the legitimate role of orderly candidate selection, without validating every deadline.

### Constitutional allocation of presidential electors

#### Igartua De La Rosa v. United States

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** 2002-02-19.

##### Whether a federal court may order Puerto Rico to appoint presidential electors

**Holding:** Article II allocates presidential electors to States, and the Twenty-Third Amendment separately allocates electors to the District of Columbia. Citizenship alone supplies Puerto Rico no additional electoral unit, number of electors or appointment-and-counting authority; a federal court therefore cannot order the territorial appointment and count sought here.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, supplies nine direct votes for the rule and disposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The rejected treaty and UOCAVA grounds were not appealed and are not revived. Congressional representation, territorial statehood and the local-law validity of Law 403 are outside the question reviewed. Participation through a former State's already allocated electors is a different claim.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The First Circuit's vacatur and direction to dismiss the preserved territorial-elector claim with prejudice are affirmed unanimously. A locally authorized nonbinding vote and a distinct claim for absentee voting through an existing State's electors are not prohibited or adjudicated.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The constitutional entitlement is rejected on its merits, not through a categorical political-question bar to territorial-rights litigation. No racial or cultural premise, general territorial immunity or reconsideration of unrelated Insular Cases holdings is adopted.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- McPherson v. Blacker, 146 U.S. 1: applied for Article II's allocation of elector appointment to States.
- Rice v. Cayetano, February 23, 2000: its prohibition on racial exclusion from a public state electorate remains; it does not create another electoral unit.
- U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton / Bryant v. Hill, May 22, 1995: fixed congressional qualifications remain distinct from creating an office or appointing unit.
- Saenz v. Roe, May 17, 1999: equal citizenship on establishing bona fide residence in a State does not allocate presidential electors to a territory.
- Bush v. Palm Beach County Canvassing Board, December 4, 2000, and Bush v. Gore, December 12, 2000: their rules for existing presidential appointment and counting retain their scope.

### Equal access to a retained former-state presidential franchise

#### Romeu v. Cohen

**Docket or dockets:** Lower-court Nos. 00-6287 and 00-6303; no Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** 2002-02-19.

For prospective reviewability in Romeu v. Cohen, February 19, 2002, lower-court Nos. 00-6287 and 00-6303, see Federal Courts: Justiciability — Prospective review of recurring presidential absentee exclusion.

##### UOCAVA as a federal minimum rather than a ceiling on state absentee eligibility

**Holding:** UOCAVA sets a minimum for its covered overseas voters and does not prohibit broader state eligibility, but that floor does not itself dispose of the independently pleaded federal equality challenge.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Souter's opinion, joined by all nine Justices, controls.

##### Equal protection reaches complete exclusion within the retained state presidential franchise

**Holding:** An applicant who establishes otherwise comparable qualification for New York's retained former-resident presidential electorate and complete exclusion from presidential participation because of relocation to Puerto Rico suffers a severe electoral burden. The State must show that its exclusion is narrowly drawn to advance a compelling electoral interest; the asserted membership, administrative and incremental-accommodation interests do not justify this exclusion.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of Souter's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg, controls the state holding and its as-applied relief.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The trigger combines otherwise comparable former-state qualification with complete presidential exclusion. Territorial residence alone does not trigger strict scrutiny, and no permanent franchise for every emigrant is created. Ordinary identification, former-residence and authentication requirements remain available.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The state injunction must prevent the responsible New York election official from denying an otherwise qualified Romeu access to the existing presidential absentee program because of Puerto Rico residence, abode or domicile, registration, or voting in local elections. It must also disapply the departure-from-the-United-States formulation insofar as that formulation would independently exclude him despite his last relevant state domicile in New York. These qualifications are unenforceable in this application; the decree does not delete them throughout every federal-election provision.

The lower court must determine the remaining ordinary former-residence, age, registration and authentication facts and implement prospective equal access. A restriction against a second presidential vote remains permissible; Puerto Rico's local vote is not such a vote. New York may not equalize by withdrawing ballots required by UOCAVA's continuing overseas minimum. Relief operates through New York's existing electors, creates no territorial electors, orders no change to another State's program and reopens no completed election.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **Anderson v. Celebrezze, 460 U.S. 780:** Its actual-burden, precise-interest and necessity inquiry is applied to the retained former-resident presidential opportunity.
- **Burdick v. Takushi, 504 U.S. 428:** Its calibrated framework is extended to this selective former-resident franchise; its effective-route holding remains controlling for candidacies in its complete-system setting.
- **McDonald v. Board of Election Commissioners, 394 U.S. 802:** Distinguished because its record did not establish exclusion from voting itself; it remains authority for the absentee distinction it reviewed.
- **Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections, 383 U.S. 663:** Its equality protection within an available franchise supports scrutiny of this selective distribution.
- **Reynolds v. Sims, 377 U.S. 533:** Its protection of meaningful electoral equality supports the participation inquiry without creating territorial electors.
- **Carrington v. Rash, 380 U.S. 89:** Its distinction between bona fide residence rules and impermissible electoral exclusions remains; it creates no permanent former-state franchise.
- **McPherson v. Blacker, 146 U.S. 1:** Its state-based appointment structure remains in force; relief uses New York's existing electors.
- **Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New Party, April 28, 1997:** Its rule requiring meaningful official recognition of a qualified party's genuine nomination remains; it does not decide complete presidential exclusion.
- **Schrader v. Blackwell, December 10, 2001:** Its truthful-designation holding for a candidate already on the ballot is distinguished; the complete-system inquiry remains operative.
- **The Bush election decisions:** Their adjudicated counting and institutional holdings remain; neither supplies a categorical answer to this former-resident eligibility classification.

##### The federal minimum must satisfy the same electoral equality requirement

**Holding:** Through the Fifth Amendment's equality protection, UOCAVA's preservation of presidential absentee eligibility for comparable former residents abroad cannot completely exclude Romeu solely because he resides in Puerto Rico unless the exclusion satisfies the same compelling-interest and narrow-tailoring requirement. It does not; a prospective as-applied declaration against the responsible federal officer is required.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of Souter's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg, controls.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The federal declaration, directed to the responsible federal officer, must state that UOCAVA's overseas-voter definitions in §1973ff-6(5)(B) and (C) may not be applied to deny an otherwise comparably qualified Romeu the presidential absentee eligibility preserved for former residents abroad solely because he resides in Puerto Rico. That direction includes the departure-linked former-domicile condition insofar as it recreates the same exclusion despite his last relevant state domicile in New York before moving to Puerto Rico. The declaration operates as applied; it does not deem Puerto Rico foreign or redefine the United States throughout the Act.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision adopts no alternative rational-basis holding or suspect classification for territorial residence. The federal overseas minimum remains operative, with ordinary qualifications preserved.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **Harris v. Rosario, 446 U.S. 651:** Distinguished at its congressional-benefits holding; it is not overruled or made the rule for every territorial voting classification.

##### The independent theories create no permanent right to the former State's ballot

**Holding:** The asserted Article IV, travel and general due-process theories do not independently entitle Romeu to carry New York electoral membership permanently after leaving the State. They supply no additional remedy on these facts; the Fifth Amendment equality claim is separately sustained.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part IV of Souter's opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, controls this rejection. Stone-Zsela does not reach it.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Rejection of these independent entitlement theories neither affirms either equality dismissal nor defeats the separate equality holding. Statehood, congressional representation, territorial electors and a future amended absentee program are not decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **Saenz v. Roe, May 17, 1999:** Its equal-citizenship rule at the new state residence remains; it supplies no independent permanent former-state electoral membership.

### Official party designations and recognition requirements

#### Schrader v. Blackwell

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket stated; reviewed judgment: 241 F.3d 783 (6th Cir. 2001).

**Decided:** December 10, 2001.

For Schrader v. Blackwell, December 10, 2001, concerning the continuing controversy, see Federal Courts: Justiciability — Recurring ballot-designation restrictions and election mootness.

##### Truthful designation of a verified, petition-qualified party nominee

**Holding:** Under Anderson-Burdick, where Ohio's ballot prints party designations, a candidate who qualified by petition and was genuinely nominated by a party may not be forced to appear as an independent without a substantial justification grounded in the actual burden and the State's demonstrated ballot interests; full party recognition is not, by itself, that justification. Ohio may verify the affiliation, distinguish recognized parties from candidate-specific nominating associations and choose truthful wording, and it need not print a label that falsely implies recognized-party nomination. The exact label is left to the remedy stage.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's opinion on the merits, joined by Stone-Zsela, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; five Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Independent access and campaigning lessen rather than eliminate the associational burden, which is less than severe. Ohio may verify affiliation, distinguish recognized parties from candidate-specific nominating associations, choose truthful wording and refuse labels that falsely imply recognized-party nomination; a demonstrated administrative or effective-governing interest connected to the restriction remains available. The rule does not eliminate party-recognition thresholds, confer recognized-party privileges or order a particular label.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The reviewed ballot-designation judgment is vacated and the case remanded, 5–4, for determination of the truthful designation, verification and administrative fit, with appropriately bounded prospective relief; the completed 1998 election is not reopened.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Anderson v. Celebrezze, 460 U.S. 780, and Burdick v. Takushi, 504 U.S. 428: the actual burden, precise interests and proportional fit remain controlling; Burdick's alternative-route holding concerns access and is not transferred to labels.
- Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New Party, No. 95-1608: its rule requiring meaningful official recognition of a qualified party's genuine nomination is distinguished because the party here lacked recognition; its treatment of a genuine nomination as central association informs the burden.
- Norman v. Reed, 502 U.S. 279: its protection of authorized party identity and independently established support supports the weight given to the verified nomination; party-recognition thresholds remain.
- Tashjian v. Republican Party of Connecticut, 479 U.S. 208, and Eu v. San Francisco County Democratic Central Committee, 489 U.S. 214: associational protection supports a truthful designation, without compelling every requested ballot format.

### Advance casting and the federal final-selection date

#### Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Keisling

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket supplied; review of 259 F.3d 1169 (9th Cir. 2001).
**Decided:** May 13, 2002.

##### Whether advance congressional voting violates the federal election day

**Holding:** Then-operative 2 U.S.C. §§1 and 7 do not preempt advance ballot casting when the State's congressional election remains open through the prescribed day and the final legal selection is completed on that day. Oregon's system, with continuing election-day voting, receipt required by that day and no earlier legally final winner, satisfies the rule; the same protection covers a materially equivalent advance-ballot feature, while a genuinely earlier final selection remains forbidden.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, unanimous.

**Material application:** Oregon accepts election-day votes and requires receipt by that day; no winner becomes legally final earlier. The proportion cast early is not controlling, and postponing counting or certification cannot cure an already final earlier selection.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision neither extends the receipt deadline nor decides late ballots or an independent constitutional entitlement to a voting method. Federal presidential absentee provisions do not expressly authorize every congressional practice.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm the judgment rejecting congressional preemption; no replacement election calendar is required.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Foster v. Love is applied to distinguish preliminary participation from legally consummated congressional selection. Its prohibition of an early final election and its allowance for compatible preliminary proceedings remain controlling; no comprehensive code for all election procedures is created.

##### Whether advance casting prematurely appoints presidential electors

**Holding:** Then-operative 3 U.S.C. §1 fixes the day on which the State's presidential-elector selection is legally completed, rather than requiring each preliminary ballot act to occur that day. Advance casting under Oregon's election-day participation and receipt conditions does not appoint electors early; the rule does not authorize an earlier legally final appointment or decide ballots first received after the prescribed deadline.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, unanimous; this is an independent construction of 3 U.S.C. §1.

**Material application:** Then-42 U.S.C. §1973aa-1(d) protects duly qualified residents absent from their district or unit on election day, and subsection (g) permits less restrictive practices. Those provisions coexist with common-day completion; they neither govern every federal office nor dispense with the appointment date. Universal advance voting does not require each voter to qualify independently under the federal absentee rule.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No permission for late receipt, earlier final appointment or replacement of the enacted state scheme follows.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm rejection of presidential-election preemption on the existing receipt and election-day participation conditions.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Foster's completion distinction is applied by analogy while its congressional scope remains intact. No prior presidential timing decision is enlarged into a permission for late receipt, early final appointment or replacement of an enacted state scheme.

#### Balderas v. Texas, 536 U.S. 919

**Docket or dockets:** No. 01-1196.
**Decided:** 2002-06-17.

##### Capacity and independently sufficient grounds

**Holding:** A preserved Section 2 district-formation claim by one protected group may satisfy the first Gingles condition in a lawful, geographically compact district either through a numerical majority or rigorous proof of dependable crossover support sufficient to elect the group's preferred candidates. Numerical exclusivity cannot defeat that supported alternative, but cohesion, majority bloc voting ordinarily sufficient to defeat the group's preferred candidates absent special circumstances such as an unopposed minority candidate, causation, and unequal opportunity under an independent totality inquiry remain necessary; an erroneous numerical screen warrants relief only when material to the disposition, and a genuinely independent sufficient lawful ground remains effective.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's signed opinion on summary direct appeal, joined by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; five direct votes for the complete rule and limited mandate.

**Material application:** The majority-linked explanation for rejecting the additional Latino-opportunity arrangement did not sufficiently identify a lawful independent disposition of the disputed capacity and geography evidence. Appellate explanations cannot supply missing trial-court findings. Rule 52(a) requires a reviewable application of the correct standard, not discussion of every exhibit.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Electoral results do not conclusively prove dependable capacity, and geometric scores do not determine legal compactness. Facts about Plan 1099C cannot be transferred without support to Plan 1123C. Failure to prove cohesion between distinct minority groups does not resolve one group’s dependable outside support. The Court decides no distinct-group or influence-only entitlement, universal population denominator or statistical formula, and does not find the statutory elements proved.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Valdespino’s two capacity routes and survival of independent lawful grounds are applied. Gingles and Growe retain the causal conditions; De Grandy requires an independent totality inquiry without maximization or a proportionality safe harbor. Growe preserves priority for timely lawful state plans, and Voinovich permits compelled districts only to remedy proved violations. Federal authorship does not exempt a replacement map from Section 2.

##### Remedy for the deficient explanation

**Holding:** Because the majority-linked explanation does not sufficiently identify a lawful ground independently disposing of the appealed additional Latino-opportunity arrangement, the congressional judgment is vacated only insofar as it rejects that arrangement. The remand requires application of both capacity routes and the remaining statutory conditions with sufficiently identified findings, while Plan 1151C remains operative unless lawfully modified and any 2002 election already conducted under Plan 1151C is left undisturbed.

**Proposition-level authority:** The same five-Justice opinion; the mandate is expressly reasoned, not inferred from an unexplained summary action.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Vacatur reaches only rejection of the appealed arrangement and affected districts. Supported findings and the plaintiffs’ burden remain; supplementation follows ordinary procedural rules. The mandate requires neither an additional district nor general reopening of trial. The obsolete thirty-seat map does not revive, and the separate Texas House and Senate judgments remain unaffected.

#### Utah v. Evans, 536 U.S. 452

**Docket or dockets:** No. 01-714.
**Decided:** 2002-06-20.

For the June 20, 2002 holding in No. 01-714 on standing and likely redress after census transmission and certification, see Federal Courts: Justiciability.

##### The Census Act permits this residual completion method

**Holding:** Sections 141 and 195 permit hot-deck imputation that completes particular unresolved units with nearby comparable information after genuine mail and field enumeration. This residual method does not select a representative sample to substitute for enumeration of a larger unenumerated population, and §195 does not prohibit it; its small percentage alone supplies no permission.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of Breyer's opinion of the Court is adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer: seven direct votes.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The method completes identified unresolved address, occupancy and household-size entries after attempts to enumerate them individually. Function, rather than timing, randomness or small scale alone, distinguishes it from representative sampling. Materially different designs and a general permission-versus-duty construction of §195 remain undecided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Department of Commerce v. United States House of Representatives: its permission for two identified designs remains intact; the four-Justice general construction does not control this independent method-specific analysis.

##### The explained method reasonably serves enumeration and geographic representation

**Holding:** The Enumeration Clause permits this residual imputation because it supplements a genuine population-counting effort and bears an explained reasonable relationship to enumeration and population-based representation. Locality and comparable housing type support the inference on this record without proof of quantified geographic superiority; a national-total improvement alone, a fixed percentage or unsupported geographic assumptions would not supply that relationship.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of Breyer's opinion of the Court is adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: six direct votes. Thomas opposes; O'Connor and Scalia do not reach this component.

**Material application:** Nearby donors of comparable housing type supply the inference, and each unresolved unit remains at its own geographic location. The record does not establish quantified improvement in distributive accuracy; the method nevertheless has the required explained geographic relationship.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Discriminatory manipulation, unsupported geographic proxies and the absence of genuine enumeration fall outside the permission. No freestanding APA merits claim is presented.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The district-court judgment is affirmed and the challenged count and allocation remain in place. No replacement count, seat transfer or new census is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Wisconsin v. City of New York: applied without changing its reasonable-relationship standard or requiring empirical certainty. Department of Commerce v. United States House of Representatives: applied for constitutional permission to supplement a genuine enumeration with supported inference. Franklin v. Massachusetts: its supported counting choices remain consistent with this application; its separate administrative-review rule is unchanged.

#### Page v. Bartels, 144 F. Supp. 2d 346 (judgment below)

**Docket or dockets:** District-court No. 01-1733.
**Decided:** 2002-06-20.

##### The constitutional inquiry concerns a protected interest and the operation impairing it

**Holding:** Racial consideration or predominance in a common territorial electorate does not itself establish a constitutional deprivation. The constitutional claims presented here must identify the governmental operation impairing a protected political interest and satisfy that claim's own elements; voters of every race receive the same protection, and Section 2 claims proceed independently on their statutory elements.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Stone-Zsela's signed opinion of the Court is adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: five direct votes. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas do not join this part.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Intentional dilution requires purpose, material impairment of protected electoral opportunity and causation. A participation claim requires an identified protected activity and concrete material impairment attributable to the challenged racial treatment or prohibited purpose; electoral defeat and total exclusion are unnecessary. A technical change or disappointment about political leverage is insufficient. No comprehensive rule for unpresented partisan or regional-separation theories is adopted.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Shaw v. Reno, Johnson v. Miller and Easley v. Cromartie: reaffirmed at their established territorial-design boundary and protection of independent injuries. The actual statutory inquiry remains governed by Section 2 and its own precedents.

##### The statutory dilution claim fails on the relevant opposing-bloc evidence

**Holding:** Section 2 does not require retention of a numerical-majority district where, on supported findings concerning the affected electorate and relevant nomination and election stages, challengers fail to establish opposing-bloc voting ordinarily sufficient to defeat the protected group's preferred candidates after considering relevant crossover support and special circumstances. Failure of that necessary condition disposes of this claim without deciding the first capacity condition or the remaining totality inquiry.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of Stone-Zsela's signed opinion of the Court is adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: seven direct votes. Scalia and Thomas agree only in the statutory judgment on their noncoverage ground.

**Material application:** Supported local election and nomination findings establish opportunity in Districts 27 and 34, even without Hispanic support. The decrease in District 27's Black voting-age population does not independently prove lost opportunity; gains elsewhere and a successful candidate's race would not answer the local inquiry.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Plaintiffs bear the ordinary preponderance burden. Valdespino's rigorous-support requirement concerns reliability, not a heightened burden or compulsory research protocol. The first capacity condition, remaining totality inquiry, distinct-group aggregation and influence-only entitlement are not decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Gingles and Voinovich: applied to the independently necessary opposing-bloc condition. Valdespino: both capacity routes remain intact without a new capacity determination. De Grandy: preserved against maximization, numerical shortcuts and statewide-offset reasoning. Balderas: its limited-remand ruling does not displace the independently sufficient findings identified here.

##### The intentional statutory claim also fails on this record

**Holding:** The separately pleaded intentional Section 2 claim fails because supported findings establish neither purposeful diminution of minority voting rights nor the actual impairment asserted. This ground is separate from the results claim and does not make intent necessary for a Section 2 results violation.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of Stone-Zsela's signed opinion of the Court is adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: seven direct votes. Scalia and Thomas agree only in the statutory judgment on their noncoverage ground.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Racial awareness and changing population percentages do not alone establish purposeful diminution. Supported trial findings receive clear-error review, and the statutory results claim remains independent of intent.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** The existing Section 2 results framework remains independent. Voinovich preserves claim-specific proof and does not make all statutory protection depend on purpose.

##### The actual dilution and participation theories fail on supported findings

**Holding:** Intentional dilution and materially unequal political participation require proof of the unlawful purpose or treatment, material impairment and causal connection belonging to the actual claim. The supported findings rejecting both loss of electoral opportunity and the separately alleged chilling of participation defeat these claims; the absence of established discriminatory purpose provides an additional ground.

**Proposition-level authority:** The constitutional application in Stone-Zsela's signed opinion is adopted by all nine Justices: Part III addresses the Fourteenth Amendment and Part IV the Fifteenth Amendment. This complete agreement on the confined applications does not enlarge the five-Justice coalition for Part I.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A prohibited purpose need not be sole or predominant. Once it is established as a substantial or motivating factor, the government must prove by a preponderance that materially the same decision would have occurred without it. That predicate was not established here. The separately rejected participation-chilling allegation cannot be answered solely by a candidate's ability to win; no developed separate due-process claim is presented.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Easley: its protection of independently asserted dilution and participation claims is applied; no reconsideration of the distinct territorial-design rule is necessary. Arlington Heights, Feeney and Brooks: their purpose and burden rules remain intact; no established prohibited-purpose predicate triggers the latter burden here.

##### The Fifteenth Amendment claim fails without deciding dilution coverage

**Holding:** Assuming the Fifteenth Amendment reaches the asserted dilution theory, the supported absence of purposeful racial abridgment defeats this claim. The Court leaves the broader coverage question open and affirms the denial of relief on this component.

**Proposition-level authority:** The constitutional application in Stone-Zsela's signed opinion is adopted by all nine Justices: Part III addresses the Fourteenth Amendment and Part IV the Fifteenth Amendment. This complete agreement on the confined applications does not enlarge the five-Justice coalition for Part I.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The final three-judge denial of injunctive relief on Counts I–IV is affirmed. The decision orders no redistricting, added district, election postponement or new trial, and supplies no immunity from another independently established wrong.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Voinovich: applied for the assumed-coverage, failed-purpose route; the Fifteenth Amendment coverage reservation remains effective.

#### Robertson v. Bartels, 534 U.S. 1110

**Docket or dockets:** No. 01-721; district-court No. 01-2024.
**Decided:** 2002-06-20.

For the June 20, 2002 holding in No. 01-721 rejecting the stated nonparty-preclusion ground, see Federal Courts.

##### The territorial-design count identifies no independent constitutional deprivation

**Holding:** Predominantly racial design of a common territorial electorate does not alone establish a Fourteenth Amendment deprivation. Even giving these plaintiffs the favorable reasonable inferences required on summary judgment, Count I identifies no independently cognizable denial or abridgment; the judgment denying relief on that count therefore stands.

**Proposition-level authority:** Parts II and III of Stone-Zsela's signed opinion of the Court are adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: five direct votes. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas dissent from the merits disposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The plaintiffs receive favorable reasonable racial-motive inferences under summary-judgment procedure; ordinary map shape or the existence of other criteria does not establish that race could not predominate. The governing substantive rule makes that disputed relative weight immaterial to the design-only claim. No second governmental act, electoral defeat or financial loss is required to show an independently cognizable wrong. The broader Fifteenth Amendment dilution-coverage question remains open.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Shaw, Miller and Easley: applied without changing the territorial-design boundary or protections for actual independent wrongs. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby: applied to favorable reasonable inferences, with materiality determined by the governing substantive law. Voinovich: its broader Fifteenth Amendment coverage reservation remains intact.

##### The actual incumbent-prospect claim concerns the same territorial operation

**Holding:** A claim that district boundaries favor minority incumbents' reelection prospects does not become a separate racial allocation of candidacy or civic rights merely by describing those prospects as an incumbent benefit. Count II identifies the composition of the common electorate and its expected political support, without an independent eligibility restriction or participation impairment, and fails under the same constitutional boundary.

**Proposition-level authority:** Parts II and III of Stone-Zsela's signed opinion of the Court are adopted by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: five direct votes. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas dissent from the merits disposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The actual counts identify no separate racial ballot qualification, restriction on candidacy, entitlement to office, official racial ballot label or independent participation barrier. Independent discrimination is not excused because an incumbent has no right to a future term. Count III's separate residency dispute cannot enlarge this appeal.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Denial of relief on Counts I and II is affirmed, 5–4, on the independent merits ground. The separate residency count is unaffected; no replacement plan, election change or new trial is required.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Easley: applied to the actual operation and preserved independent injuries. Anderson v. Martin: distinguished from common geographical composition. Adarand: preserved for an actual covered racial allocation, without using its justification rule to create one.

#### Missouri Republican Party v. Lamb

**Docket or dockets:** Eighth Circuit Nos. 00-1773 and 00-2686 (270 F.3d 567).
**Decided:** June 27, 2002.

##### Actual candidate resources remain distinct from independent and joint expression

**Holding:** A State may regulate actual party-to-candidate resource transfers and genuine contribution conduits under the contribution standard: government must establish an objectively grounded, sufficiently important corruption or circumvention interest and a restriction closely drawn to it while preserving meaningful association and effective advocacy. Party identity, shared objectives, endorsement or ordinary access alone does not establish an actual candidate-resource connection or corruption; genuinely independent expression remains protected.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I. Opinion of the Court (Stone-Zsela), unanimous at the actual candidate-resource and genuine-conduit scope; Kennedy, Scalia and Thomas retain their separate view of joint expression without withholding a join here.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Buckley’s resource/independent-expression distinction and Colorado I’s actual candidate-connection requirement govern. Colorado II supplies neither a universal classification of jointly developed messages nor automatic validation of every party ceiling.

##### The federal record establishes a relevant preventive interest beyond formal earmarking

**Holding:** Relevant experience outside the State may establish an objective preventive justification without a completed local scandal, mandatory new local study or proof that legislators subjectively relied on that evidence when acting. Here the federal record establishes a materially relevant risk that tacit donor-party-candidate understandings and fundraising credits can circumvent valid candidate limits despite formal earmarking attribution; that resolved interest does not by itself establish close fit of Missouri's actual ceilings.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part II of the unanimous opinion.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision establishes the relevant preventive interest, not donor-specific attribution or corruption in every transfer. A tally, ordinary political agreement or access alone is insufficient.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Colorado II’s informal-circumvention record applies to tacit understandings and fundraising credits. Formal earmarking remains useful but is not an exclusive response. Renton’s outside-evidence analogy does not replace the contribution-specific constitutional test.

##### Missouri must justify its actual ceilings while preserving meaningful association

**Holding:** Missouri bears the separate burden to connect the supported circumvention risk to the actual operation and amounts of its challenged party ceilings, showing close fit that preserves meaningful chosen-party association and effective candidate-connected support. A federal ceiling's validity, unlimited independent spending or challengers' failure to prove that expression becomes practically inaudible does not discharge that burden; no fixed dollar floor or universal numerical safe harbor governs.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part III of the unanimous opinion.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Russell requires government to justify actual operation and preserve meaningful association; Shrink’s supported statewide individual ceiling establishes no numerical safe harbor or challenger-impossibility burden. Day protects the chosen intermediary, without treating other speakers or channels as an answer. Colorado II’s particular federal Senate ceiling does not validate materially lower Missouri amounts as a matter of law. Daggett retains the affirmative government burden and Mariani the distinction between direct candidate resources and different financing arrangements.

##### Vacatur requires a fit decision and corresponding relief within the presented scope

**Holding:** The reviewed judgment cannot stand on automatic validation by Colorado II or a burden on challengers to prove practically ineffective expression. It is vacated and the case remanded for findings or record-based conclusions connecting the already supported mechanism to the actual Missouri ceilings, followed by appropriate relief for any limits the State cannot justify; adequate existing evidence may suffice without a new study or compulsory trial.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part IV of the unanimous opinion.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Severability requires its proper record. The separate reliance or prior-restraint contention and unpresented discrimination claim are outside review. No replacement dollar amount, blanket invalidation, retrospective liability or mandatory new evidence collection follows.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Vacate and remand, 9–0. The already-established preventive interest is not reopened; the receiving court must justify actual ceilings and give appropriate relief for any that the State cannot sustain, using adequate existing proof where sufficient.


### Legislative population deviations and independent racial-injury proof

#### Montiel v. Davis

**Docket or dockets:** District Court No. 01-0447-BH-S; judgment below, 215 F. Supp. 2d 1279; no Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** January 13, 2003.

##### Whether sub-ten-percent legislative deviations or nonexclusive discriminatory purpose foreclose a challenge

**Holding:** A state legislative maximum population deviation below ten percent does not alone establish a prima facie violation, but remains challengeable through proof of arbitrary or discriminatory weighting.
