The actual Law School program satisfies that same-right guarantee, so the presented §1981 policy challenge fails independently of the constitutional and Title VI dispositions.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: six Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Academic freedom does not excuse exclusion. Section 1983 supplies an authorized enforcement route without changing the admissions standard; causes, proper defendants and remedies remain separate.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Runyon supplies educational-contract coverage and rejects an associational defense to exclusion; McDonald protects every race; General Building Contractors addresses intentional discrimination without turning every constitutional permission into a statutory defense.

### Private adult intimacy and selective criminal punishment

#### Lawrence v. Texas, 539 U.S. 558

**Docket or dockets:** No. 02-102.
**Decided:** June 26, 2003.

##### Constitutional liberty against criminal punishment of private consensual adult intimacy

**Holding:** Fourteenth Amendment liberty protects private consensual sexual intimacy between adults against criminal punishment justified solely by moral disapproval of that intimacy. Bowers v. Hardwick is overruled to the extent it permits that punishment. Convictions and penalties imposed on that basis must be removed; an evenhanded prohibition of the same protected conduct cannot cure the violation.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, supported directly by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The protected category excludes coercion, conduct involving minors, public conduct and commercial sex. Civil relationship status is not decided. No express fundamental-right classification, compelling-necessity test or collateral-review rule has controlling support here.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Both convictions and their dependent penalties must be vacated, and these prosecutions terminated. The rule applies in covered nonfinal prosecutions and direct appeals through the lawful procedures governing each case.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Bowers loses authority for punishment within the defined category. Griswold and Eisenstadt supply individual intimate-choice principles; Casey supplies protected choice and a justification-based approach to overruling without exporting its abortion framework. Glucksberg is distinguished by its concrete protective reasons concerning assisted death and is not read as prescribing an exclusive historical-description method. Romer's former preservation of Bowers yields to this express overruling. The inadequacy of Bowers's description of the liberty, continued criminal intrusion and conflict with individual-choice principles support departure; comparable settled transactional reliance is absent.

##### Independent equal-protection defect in the selective same-sex criminal penalty

**Independent alternative holding:** Ordinary rational-basis review forbids this additional criminal penalty for same-sex participants when otherwise comparable private consensual adult conduct is unpunished and the distinction bears no rational relationship to a legitimate reason for the added disadvantage. The challenger retains the burden of negating a reasonably conceivable legitimate explanation; it is met because disapproval of the class does not establish a separate injury from the matched conduct.

**Proposition-level authority for alternative holding:** Part II of Ginsburg's Court opinion, supported directly by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; seven Justices independently require the same conviction remedy.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Because the selective penalty fails even ordinary review, the Court need not decide whether this same-sex distinction is a sexual-orientation classification subject to Shahar's intermediate scrutiny, and the comparison creates no general rule excluding moral interests from legislation. Ordinary review still permits imperfect classifications, reasonable generalizations and conceivable grounds without formal findings, empirical certainty or a least-restrictive-means inquiry.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Romer requires a rational connection to the particular unequal disadvantage. Heller preserves the challenger's burden and ordinary legislative latitude. Moreno and Cleburne supply the limits on bare harm and irrational prejudice. Authority to regulate conduct generally does not answer the independent discriminatory-penalty question. Shahar v. Bowers's intermediate scrutiny is not reached because the selective penalty fails even ordinary review.


### Abortion-facility qualifications and identified inspection records

#### Greenville Women's Clinic v. Commissioner — qualifications and patient information

**Docket or dockets:** Fourth Circuit Nos. 01-2090 and 01-2235; judgment below, 317 F.3d 357.
**Decided:** October 27, 2003.

For the clergy question in Greenville Women's Clinic v. Commissioner, October 27, 2003, Nos. 01-2090 and 01-2235, see First Amendment — Religious arrangements in facility licensing; for notice and residual sanctions, see Administrative Law — Ascertainable medical-facility duties and residual sanctions.

##### Whether medical cooperation and secular referrals confer an arbitrary private veto

**Holding:** States may require objective medical qualifications and emergency-care arrangements, but may not make protected care depend on an outsider's arbitrary, legally uncontrolled licensing consent. The separately considered medical and secular-referral provisions, in their established operation here, have not been shown to create that veto.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part I, unanimous on the qualification and arbitrary-control ground; this agreement does not establish unanimous assent to Casey's complete residual-interference framework.

**Material application:** Section 205(C)(2) requires a signed agreement with a board-certified obstetrician/gynecologist if none is on staff; that physician must be able to admit patients at a local hospital offering obstetrical and gynecological services and be available throughout operating hours. Section 305(A) separately requires staff and consulting physicians' privileges at local hospitals providing appropriate obstetrical and gynecological services, permitting documented Department-approved emergency-transfer arrangements when hospitalization becomes necessary. Section 309(B) independently commands appropriate local hospital privileges; neither other provision's exception transfers to it. No actual or supported impending arbitrary refusal controlling these providers is established. Section 307's secular referrals provide services as needed.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Existing licenses evidence operation but do not require waiting for closure before challenging a supported prospective veto. A discretionary community-health-and-welfare waiver is no assured timely cure; public-hospital constraints do not automatically bind private institutions. Earlier overall-access and equal-protection judgments are outside review.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm rejection of this delegation claim.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Yick Wo prohibits arbitrary licensing control. Danforth and Casey govern effective third-party control of protected choice without making professional cooperation itself a private veto.

##### What permits governmental access to intimate clinical information

**Holding:** Authorized transfer of intimate clinic records to inspectors requires a sufficient connection between the regulatory need and the information, recipients, official function, scope, uses and safeguards. Courts must determine those permissions and connections, restrain established improper access or dissemination and preserve lawful confidential inspection.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part IV-A, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer; six reasoning joins. Stone-Zsela supplies a seventh vote for vacatur and remand on a separate ground only.

**Material application:** Identified care audits, complaint investigation and corroboration may serve sufficiently connected tasks. Section 102(F)(2) limits copying to documents required for inspections or investigations, without resolving all access permissions. Section 401 includes contact, social-security, birth, family and emergency-contact fields, so name deletion may leave identification possible. Retention, training and privacy protections must be considered with actual use and redistribution permissions. Reported releases require assessment without establishing every release's details or authority.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 44-7-310's public-identification restriction has facility-licensure, certificate-of-need, employee-licensing and court-order exceptions. Section 44-7-315 requires disclosure on written request while protecting identities of individuals present in a licensed facility. Section 44-41-60 excludes patient and physician names from registrar reports; section 44-41-360 separately requires an explicit constitutional anonymity determination absent the woman's consent. These distinct rules do not establish universal inspection secrecy. Redaction, consent and targeted follow-up are alternatives to assess where adequate, not universal preconditions. Universal compelling need is not the governing rule.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Vacate and remand, 7–2, for actual-permission, regulatory-connection and safeguard determinations. The District Court's universal compelling-need restriction and appellate categorical rejection cease to be final merits resolutions. Existing material may suffice without another hearing; ordinary equity governs surviving interim requests, preserving severable lawful requirements.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lawall's information-recipient-function inquiry extends to clinic-to-inspector access. Herring requires recipient-specific assessment of further dissemination. Doe's confined benefits-administration ruling does not decide these permissions and retains its rejection of universal indispensability. Whalen preserves safeguarded health administration; Casey's bounded reporting holdings confer no general identified-access permission.

##### When inspection duties also implicate protected reproductive choice

**Holding:** Proved additional interference caused by an actual inspection obligation independently invokes Casey's complete framework. The claimant must identify the duty, affected population, attributable burden and applicable protection; relief must address the violation while preserving lawful requirements.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part IV-B, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer; five direct joins. Kennedy's Part IV-A join does not extend to this rationale.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A prohibited baseline invasion, effective private veto, denial of timely necessary care, obstructive purpose or substantial obstacle is independently invalid. Other severe interference requires compelling permissible justification and narrow tailoring; other meaningful interference requires substantiated justification and fit addressing concrete practicable substantially less burdensome alternatives. Usable exceptions and supported prospective effects matter; success for some patients cannot erase another group's demonstrated burden. Below meaningful interference, the heightened access inquiry ends while independent protections remain. Clinical judgment, truthful communication and timely necessary care retain protection. Identifiers or a privacy label do not presume an access burden, and the earlier overall-access judgment is not reopened.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Apply the corresponding protection to proved additional inspection interference within the preserved claims and tailor relief accordingly.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Casey's complete framework remains unchanged and independent of information-transfer doctrine; Lawall preserves that distinction.

### Racial political-process claims concerning instructional policy

#### Valeria v. Davis

**Docket or dockets:** Ninth Circuit No. 01-15219; judgment below, 307 F.3d 1036.
**Decided:** November 25, 2003.

##### What establishes a racial barrier in relocation of educational authority

**Holding:** Predominant benefit to minority pupils does not by itself make statewide displacement of an educational program unconstitutional. The claimant must show a racial classification, deliberate racial proxy or racially selective obstruction of ordinary political participation. A prior discrimination adjudication is unnecessary, and absence of hostility does not conclusively answer an established racial decisionmaking structure.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part I, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Demographics and campaign references may bear on the mechanism but do not alone establish it; language proficiency is not automatically race. An established racial mechanism invokes Adarand's common substantial-justification standard: important lawful objective, evidence-supported substantial relationship, justified coverage and actual burdens, and an adequate response to concrete practicable alternatives comparably advancing the objective with materially less racial disadvantage. The rule protects political equality, not policy victory or access to every political level.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Hunter and Seattle protect against race-selected political burdens. Coalition for Economic Equity preserves the inquiry for lawful voluntary racial measures without a prior-remedial-decree requirement. Crawford permits neutral policy withdrawal and statewide educational authority without erasing structural review. Adarand supplies the actual racial-classification standard; Romer's class-wide exclusion from protection differs from a neutral curricular policy.

##### Whether Proposition 227 establishes that allocation on the tried record

**Holding:** Proposition 227's supported text, operation and trial findings establish a linguistic instructional policy rather than the requisite racial allocation of political authority. The facial political-process claim therefore fails.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas; five Justices. The other four join Part I only and would require further application.

**Material application:** The instructional rule applies to every family seeking the method. Immersion normally serves as a transition not exceeding one year, with mainstream instruction upon proficiency. Every waiver requires parental consent. Waivers cover existing English knowledge; a child at least ten whom the school finds would receive better English education through an alternative; or, after thirty days of immersion, identified physical, emotional, psychological or educational needs and better development through an alternative. Twenty waivers in a grade at a school require an alternative class. Amendment requires voter approval or a purpose-furthering enactment approved by two-thirds of each house and signed by the Governor. These real limitations use instruction and need rather than ancestry.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Minority concentration, Latino references in campaign materials and continued local power over other subjects establish effects and subject selection, but do not establish race as the authority rule's source on this record. The pedagogical-purpose finding reinforces rather than replaces the structural inquiry. Neutral wording alone does not defeat a supported proxy claim. Independent educational and language-access duties retain their force; statutory claims omitted from the operative complaint are not revived.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm judgment for California, 5–4, and deny the requested facial political-process injunction.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Coalition's expressly race-selected allocation is distinguished by this supported proficiency-based policy. Its structural rule remains controlling.

### Racial-impact objections to federal solicitation rules

#### McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, 540 U.S. 93 — racial-impact challenge to federal solicitation rules

**Docket or dockets:** Nos. 02-1674, 02-1675, 02-1676, 02-1702, 02-1727, 02-1733, 02-1734, 02-1740, 02-1747, 02-1753, 02-1755 and 02-1756.
**Decided:** December 10, 2003.

For the distinct questions in McConnell, December 10, 2003, on these consolidated dockets, see Election Law — campaign financing and electoral expression; Federal Courts: Justiciability — claimant-specific thresholds and regulated-party standing; First Amendment — press functions and broadcaster records; Constitutional Structure — federal election authority and reserved state powers.

##### Whether the presented Thompson racial-impact theory establishes a racial political barrier

**Holding:** The Thompson racial-impact theory fails as presented: Valeria requires an actual racial classification, deliberate proxy or racially selective political barrier, while this theory identifies demographic consequences of a uniform federal-candidate solicitation rule rather than that trigger.

**Proposition-level authority:** O’Connor’s opinion for the Court, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; eight Justices adopt this racial-impact proposition. Stone-Zsela agrees in the disposition only.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A uniform description does not insulate an actually proved racial classification, deliberate proxy or selective political barrier. The rejection concerns the demographic-impact theory presented here.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The racial-impact alternative supplies no additional relief against the federal-candidate solicitation rule.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** **Valeria:** Its racial-classification, proxy or selective-barrier rule is applied; an animus-only substitute is rejected.

#### Concrete Works of Colorado v. City and County of Denver (judgment below: 321 F.3d 950)

**Docket or dockets:** Supreme Court docket not supplied.

**Decided:** 2003-12-18.

For the preserved fit adjudication and the separate mootness dispositions, see Federal Courts and Federal Courts: Justiciability, Concrete Works of Colorado v. City and County of Denver, decided December 18, 2003, judgment below 321 F.3d 950.

##### Whether Denver proved the racial contracting provisions’ substantial justification — Concrete Works of Colorado v. City and County of Denver, 2003-12-18

**Holding:** A public contracting classification satisfies Adarand when the government proves an important lawful remedial objective and a substantial, evidence-supported relationship between the classification and that objective, accounting for its actual coverage and burdens and answering supported, practicable alternatives that would comparably advance the objective with materially less racial disadvantage. Linked statistical and anecdotal evidence can establish local exclusion to which public spending contributes without a prior discrimination judgment against each contractor or individual proof of injury to every beneficiary; Denver's developed evidence and preserved fit determination meet that burden here.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, unanimous; all nine participating Justices directly join this proposition.

**Material application:** Accepted findings, contracting experience, studies and testimony connect local exclusion with firms receiving city funds. The developed response to capacity and availability criticisms addresses hiring, subcontracting and equipment rental; the preserved fit determination remains effective.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Denver retains ultimate persuasion. General societal disparity, failure to produce a counterstudy, or proof supporting a different classification does not establish the required justification. No mandatory regression, fixed disparity cutoff, universal prior discrimination judgment or individualized injury prerequisite is imposed.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The direction to enter judgment for Denver on the live 1990 damages and 1998 prospective claims is affirmed; inconsistent injunctive and declaratory relief must be removed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Adarand supplies substantial justification; Engineering Contractors requires responsive treatment of supported practical alternatives; City of Dallas requires a demonstrated local remedial connection. Gratz requires scrutiny of actual mechanism, coverage and burdens; Grutter requires genuine consideration of practicable alternatives without exhaustion of imagined possibilities.

##### Whether the women-owned-business provisions have independent constitutional support — Concrete Works of Colorado v. City and County of Denver, 2003-12-18

**Holding:** Government must establish an actual important objective and a substantial relationship between the sex classification and that objective under the demanding governmental proof requirement. Denver satisfies that standard through the women-specific utilization, earnings and exclusion evidence and the program's preserved fit; proof supporting the racial provisions does not by itself establish this separate justification.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, unanimous; all nine participating Justices directly join this proposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The government’s demanding proof burden concerns actual objectives and the sex classification’s own relationship to them. Stereotypes and evidence about other groups cannot replace women-specific support.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Judgment for Denver on the live sex-classification challenge remains in force.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** City of Dallas preserves the separate sex-classification inquiry and requires independent evidentiary support.

#### Leebaert v. Harrington (judgment below: 332 F.3d 134)

**Docket or dockets:** No Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** 2004-02-17.

For the other questions in this decision, see First Amendment — whether combining parental and religious objections establishes heightened scrutiny of ordinary instruction.

##### Whether parental educational liberty requires an exemption from neutral compulsory instruction — Leebaert v. Harrington, 2004-02-17

**Holding:** Parental authority over upbringing and education does not confer a general constitutional right to remove a public-school pupil from neutral ordinary instruction. The rule covers genuine instruction while preserving independently protected parental and personal interests.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's unanimous opinion of the Court.

**Material application:** The stipulated dispute concerns attendance at health instruction, with the requirement's reasonable relationship to education conceded. Mere exposure to a lesson does not establish interference with a protected parental choice.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Public-school enrollment does not waive constitutional protection. The federal ruling does not determine the independent state-law exemptions.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The federal judgment and denial of the requested exemption are affirmed; dismissal of the state-law claims remains without prejudice.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Brown v. Hot, Sexy & Safer Productions supplies the compulsory-exposure boundary. Meyer v. Nebraska and Pierce v. Society of Sisters preserve parental teaching and educational choice without granting control over each public-school lesson. Elizabeth G. Curtis v. School Committee of Falmouth remains confined to its optional-program setting and did not alone decide compulsory attendance.

#### Benjamin v. Fraser, 343 F.3d 35 (judgment below)

**Docket or dockets:** No separate Supreme Court docket supplied.
**Decided:** May 20, 2004.

##### What constitutional showing governs deliberately maintained systemic pretrial conditions

**Holding:** For prospective relief from longstanding, deliberately maintained systemic pretrial conditions, detainees must prove by a preponderance a current substantial risk of serious harm and conditions unrelated reasonably to a legitimate nonpunitive purpose or excessive in relation to it. Sustained notice, a genuine opportunity to deliberate and prolonged inadequate correction establish the institutional culpability shown here without separate proof of every incumbent's subjective appreciation; negligence alone remains insufficient.

**Proposition-level authority:** Part I of Souter's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer; seven direct joins. Scalia and Thomas concur in the constitutional-relief judgment on a distinct actual-notice and knowing-nonresponse ground, not this full rationale.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Serious danger alone is insufficient without the stated deliberately maintained conditions and culpability. Individual damages and convicted-prisoner claims fall outside this prospective pretrial holding.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Bell supplies protection against punishment before conviction. Daniels excludes negligence, Crawford-El supplies ordinary civil proof without eliminating substantive elements, and County of Sacramento v. Lewis makes custodial duties and the opportunity for deliberation material without importing its emergency-pursuit standard. Farmer's knowledge and reasonable-response rule retains force for the convicted-prisoner claim it decided.

For Benjamin, decided May 20, 2004, no separate Supreme Court docket supplied, OCC classification and appointment are in Federal Courts; current prospective-relief conditions and implementation are in Federal Courts: Immunities and Remedies.

#### Jones v. R. R. Donnelley & Sons Co., 541 U.S. 369 (2004)

**Docket or dockets:** No. 02-1205.
**Decided:** May 3, 2004.

##### Whether a post-1990 amendment supplies the four-year limitation for a claim under an older statute

**Holding:** Unless another law supplies the limitation, 28 U.S.C. §1658(a)'s four-year period from accrual applies when a congressional enactment after December 1, 1990 made the asserted claim possible, including an amendment of a preexisting statute. The claimant must identify the amendment's new substantive basis for liability against the defendant; merely citing amended text or an amendment irrelevant to an already available claim does not establish the federal period.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's unanimous opinion of the Court.

**Material application:** The 1991 expansion of §1981 into performance, modification, termination and enjoyment of contractual benefits supplies the newly actionable basis for the employees' hostile-environment, termination and transfer claims insofar as each depends on that expansion. Claims within one complaint may have different limitations periods.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse the categorical rejection of §1658 based on §1981's original enactment date. Restore claims improperly barred under the shorter borrowed period, determine accrual and any disputed tolling or timeliness claim by claim, and adjudicate the surviving claims through ordinary proceedings, including the same analysis for any properly certified class.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Rivers v. Roadway Express identifies the substantive expansion and retains its prospective temporal boundary. Patterson v. McLean Credit Union supplies the earlier-text coverage against which amendment dependence is measured. Goodman v. Lukens Steel continues to require borrowing where no federal period displaces it. Landgraf's provision-specific temporal analysis remains distinct from §1658's enacted-date criterion.

#### Tennessee v. Lane, 541 U.S. 509 (2004) — Civil Rights, OT2003

**Docket or dockets:** No. 02-1667.
**Decided:** May 17, 2004.

##### What statutory conditions and defense burdens govern the judicial-access claims

**Holding:** A Title II claimant must prove qualification under §12131, disability-based exclusion, denial or discrimination under §12132, and the applicable conditions for relief under §12133. The State must substantiate a claimed fundamental alteration under the applicable regulation; the separate existing-facilities defense and its procedures apply only within their own scope.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; seven Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 35.130(b)(7) requires necessary reasonable modifications unless the entity demonstrates a fundamental alteration of the actual service, program or activity. The claimant must establish the claim and needed modification, while the State must give service-specific evidence and reasons; labels, inconvenience or unsupported cost assertions do not establish its defense.

For existing facilities, §35.150(a) requires accessibility of the service, program or activity viewed in its entirety, not necessarily each building, and does not require action threatening or destroying historic significance. Under subsection (a)(3), the entity must prove fundamental alteration or undue financial and administrative burdens; its head or designee must consider all resources available for funding and operation and issue written reasons. Even when a proposed action is excused, another action avoiding the alteration or burden must ensure receipt of the benefits or services. These financial-burden and written-reasons requirements are not imported into every §35.130(b)(7) modification claim. Section 35.150(b)(1) permits effective alternatives to structural alteration and gives priority to the most integrated appropriate setting.

**Material application:** Lane's and Jones's claims require separate proof of access, qualification, reasonable accommodations, defenses, causation and compensable injury. A physical barrier, ineffective participation and an entitlement to compensation are distinct inquiries.

For Lane, No. 02-1667, decided May 17, 2004, the court-access abrogation and effective prospective-relief holdings are in Federal Courts: Immunities and Remedies.



### Religious-diet equal protection

#### Williams v. Morton — Religious-diet equal protection

**Docket or dockets:** No separate Supreme Court docket number is supplied.
**Decided:** 2004-06-02

For Williams v. Morton, 2004-06-02, No separate Supreme Court docket number is supplied, see First Amendment for [The governing constitutional and summary-judgment standards](../HOLDINGS.md#the-governing-constitutional-and-summary-judgment-standards); [The record supports the refusal to add halal meat](../HOLDINGS.md#the-record-supports-the-refusal-to-add-halal-meat).

##### The asserted meat-based comparator lacks its factual predicate

**Holding:** An equal-protection claim premised on furnishing meat to one religious group while denying it to another requires evidence of that differential benefit. The corrected and corroborated record describes both religious diets as meatless, so the asserted meat preference supplies no triable equal-protection violation.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part III, joined by all nine Justices, is the opinion of the Court.

**Material application:** The meat description in an earlier certification was corrected and corroborated. Different aggregate spending for programs of different sizes does not establish the alleged meat preference.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Summary judgment for officials on the identified equal-protection claim is affirmed unanimously.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lukumi requires examination of actual governmental religious treatment; the asserted differential benefit is absent.

## Standards and Tests selection: Prison-conditions prospective relief

### Prison-conditions prospective relief

**Governing question:** The §3626 scope, necessity findings and preliminary-relief conditions.

**Current rule:** In a civil proceeding arising under federal law concerning conditions of confinement or officials' effects on confined persons' lives, prospective relief must be narrowly drawn, extend no further than necessary to correct the particular plaintiffs' federal-right violation and be the least intrusive necessary means; the court must make those findings and give substantial weight to adverse public-safety and criminal-justice-system effects. Relief requiring or permitting an official to exceed state or local authority or otherwise violate that law also requires that federal law require the state-law violation, necessity to correct the federal violation and absence of any other corrective relief. The statute confers no authority to build prisons or raise taxes and preserves otherwise applicable remedial limits.

Otherwise authorized preliminary injunctive relief must be narrow, no broader than necessary for the identified harm and least intrusive, with substantial safety/system weight and respect for the distinct state-law conditions. It expires ninety days after entry unless the court makes the prospective-relief findings and makes the order final before expiration. An existing permanent decree does not automatically become a preliminary order.

**Authority by component:**

- Enacted conditions, scope and all-relief transition: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §802, original 18 U.S.C. §3626(a)(1)–(2), (c)–(d), (g) and §802(b)(1), April 26, 1996.
- Existing-decree application and substantive findings: Lewis v. Casey — Holdings IV–VI, Holding IV, June 24, 1996; Kennedy Part IV for all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela joins only the statutory disposition. 
- Bounded constitutional operation of termination, not a change to the present entry’s remedial conditions: Plyler v. Moore, Plyler v. Moore — II. The prospective-relief rule preserves judicial adjudication, June 23, 1997; see the termination entry’s component authority.

- Federal-law requirement replaces federal permission; effective on enactment and in pending cases: Prison Litigation Reform Act amendments — §123(a)(1)(A) and (b), amending §3626(a)(1)(B)(i), 1997-11-26.

**Present operation effective:** Pub. L. 105-119, §123, 1997-11-26, for the federal-requirement condition; the other statutory conditions and Lewis qualifications retain their original dates.

**Controlling construction:** Prospective relief is all relief other than compensatory monetary damages. A §3626 civil prison-conditions action excludes habeas proceedings challenging the fact or duration of confinement. A prison includes federal, state and local juvenile or adult criminal detention facilities. Consent decrees include relief based wholly or partly on consent or acquiescence and must comply with subsection (a). Private settlements whose only federal judicial enforcement is reinstatement of the settled proceeding are distinct; otherwise available state breach remedies survive. Section 3626 does not govern relief a state court enters solely on state-law claims.

**Effective transition:** Amended §3626 applies to prospective relief originally granted or approved before, on or after April 26, 1996. Existing findings may meet the necessary predicates at their actual scope; ritual wording, modest cost or reasonableness alone neither establishes nor defeats compliance. Prison-conditions termination motions and automatic stays states Plyler’s June 23, 1997 resolution of the presented Article III and due-process objections to original §3626(b)(2), with the full §3626(b)(3) preservation condition. Rouse, Benjamin and Gavin apply the amended conditions within the bounds stated in Prison-conditions termination motions and automatic stays; no automatic-stay constitutional holding follows.

**Related current rules:** Prison-conditions termination motions and automatic stays states the separate actual-motion triggers; Prisoner-release orders and prison crowding supplies additional release-order requirements.

**Holdings navigation:** Lewis v. Casey, 518 U.S. 343 (1996). Plyler v. Moore (1997-06-23) — Federal Courts / Prison access and prospective relief.

**Former-rule note:** Before November 26, 1997, §3626(a)(1)(B)(i) required federal permission rather than a federal requirement for the departure from state law. Section 123 applies the revised term from enactment, including pending cases.

**Current rule — implementation of continuing obligations:** Each continued duty requires written, record-based findings of a current and ongoing federal violation and the statutory need, narrowness and least-intrusiveness conditions. Relief may exceed the bare constitutional minimum when those findings establish its remedial necessity. Government must substantiate a proposed narrower cure as adequate to correct the proved violation; its silence or failure to support an alternative does not replace the court’s independent findings. Supported orders must identify responsible officials in their official capacities, required acts and a reasonable compliance schedule, and obtain verifiable condition reports within demonstrated need and lawful authority. Duties end when their current statutory justification ceases, while a measure necessary to prevent recurrence may continue after completion of an act. Enforcement of a valid, sufficiently definite command requires the applicable notice, opportunity to respond and judicial determination.

**Authority by component — current obligations and implementation:** [Benjamin v. Fraser, May 20, 2004, Part IV.A (all nine on substantive relief and statutory conditions), Part IV.B (Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer)](../terms/OT2003/records/benjamin_v_fraser_merits_2004-05-20.md#holdings). Rufo’s equitable modification burdens are not added to the separate statutory termination route.

**Present operation effective — implementation component:** May 20, 2004; the earlier statutory predicates and dates remain effective.

## Standards and Tests selection: Statutory exhaustion and screening of prisoner conditions actions

### Statutory exhaustion and screening of prisoner conditions actions

**Governing question:** The original §1997e prefiling condition and distinct screening commands.

**Current rule:** A confined prisoner may not bring a prison-conditions action under §1983 or any other federal law until available administrative remedies are exhausted. On its own motion or a party's motion, the court shall dismiss such an action if satisfied that it is frivolous, malicious, fails to state a claim or seeks money from an immune defendant. A claim that on its face has one of those four defects may be dismissed without first requiring exhaustion. State failure to adopt or adhere to an administrative grievance procedure alone supplies no action under CRIPA §3 or §5. “Prisoner” in §1997e means a person incarcerated or detained in any facility who is accused of, convicted of, sentenced for, or adjudicated delinquent for violations of criminal law or terms or conditions of parole, probation, pretrial release or a diversionary program.

An actually accessible grievance process authorized to take responsive action concerning the complaint remains available even if it cannot award the money damages demanded. A prisoner cannot avoid the enacted exhaustion condition by requesting damages alone; lack of compensatory authority supplies no general futility exception. The permission to dismiss a facially defective claim before exhaustion remains distinct from an entitlement to nonexhausted merits adjudication.

Prison life includes individual episodes as well as general conditions, including an excessive-force claim. The requirement remains exhaustion before suit of a process actually available and authorized to respond; a process obstructed in practice or unable to respond is not made available by its formal existence. This coverage rule supplies no free-standing futility exception or new grievance-deadline, default or limitations rule.

**Authority by component:**

- Available-remedies command, screening and its prior-exhaustion exception: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §803(d), original 42 U.S.C. §1997e(a)–(c), (h), April 26, 1996.

- Availability despite inability to award requested money and distinct permissive screening: Canonical Decision Record `Booth_v_Churner_merits_2001-05-29.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / A responsive administrative process remains available although it cannot award money, 2001-05-29; O’Connor’s unanimous opinion.

- Canonical Decision Record `porter-v-nussle_merits_2002-02-26.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Exhaustion covers individual incidents of prison life, 2002-02-26; Stevens's unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Porter, February 26, 2002, for individual-episode and excessive-force coverage; Booth's responsive-process rule and original screening provisions retain their earlier dates.

**Effective transition:** The statute was enacted April 26, 1996. Section 802's express all-prospective-relief transition is not generalized to §1997e or §1915; disputed application to pending matters remains unresolved unless an applicable authority separately resolves it.

**Unresolved interaction:** McCarthy’s former damages-only BOP conclusion survives in its no-congressional-command setting and supplies no exception to the PLRA command. Neither Booth nor Porter supplies a comprehensive unavailability, procedural-default or limitations rule; Porter resolves excessive-force coverage as stated above. A nonexistent, wholly powerless or actually inaccessible process was outside its established record. Section 1915’s fee-screening mechanisms remain distinct.

**Holdings navigation:** [Booth v. Churner, 532 U.S. 731 — Prisoner litigation and available administrative processes](HOLDINGS.md#booth-v-churner-532-us-731).

## Standards and Tests selection: Serious risks in prison conditions and deliberate indifference

### Serious risks in prison conditions and deliberate indifference

**Governing question:** What objective danger, official culpability and response govern preventive prison-conditions claims and failure-to-protect liability.

**Current rule:** A prisoner may establish an Eighth Amendment violation through deliberate indifference to involuntary exposure posing an unreasonable risk of serious future harm without waiting for existing disease. For future-health exposure, the objective inquiry includes the seriousness and likelihood of harm and contemporary society’s unwillingness to tolerate the risk. For a substantial danger to inmate safety, an official must actually know facts indicating the risk, actually draw the inference and disregard it unreasonably. Constructive knowledge or negligence is insufficient. Reasonable protective action defeats deliberate-indifference liability even if harm occurs. Actual awareness may be proved circumstantially, including from an obvious risk, but obviousness permits rather than compels the inference. Deliberate avoidance of confirmation may support actual awareness; a specific prisoner warning, identification of the exact assailant or prediction of the precise time is unnecessary. Knowledge cannot be imputed collectively without proof of the individual official’s awareness. Prospective relief considers current danger and awareness through the litigation and whether unlawful disregard is likely to continue; an adequate showing of nonrecurrence may defeat that relief. Later notice can support prospective protection but does not retroactively establish awareness for damages.

**Authority by component:**

- Preventive protection does not require existing disease: Helling v. McKinney — Preventive protection does not require existing disease, 1993-06-18. White’s Opinion of the Court, Preventive protection does not require existing disease portion; Stone-Zsela, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter (7 Justices). Direct proposition-level majority; no Marks aggregation.

- Actual-awareness standard, circumstantial proof, reasonable response and preventive relief: Farmer v. Brennan — Actual awareness and unreasonable disregard of substantial danger; Circumstantial proof and reconsideration of summary judgment; Current danger governs preventive relief, 1994-06-06. Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg. Eight Justices adopt this rule; Thomas joins only the judgment. The proof-and-remand portion of Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg. Eight adopt its reasoning; all nine support vacatur and remand. The prospective-relief portion of Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg; eight Justices adopt this rule and the bounded remand.

**Present operation effective:** Farmer v. Brennan, 1994-06-06, for subjective culpability, proof and preventive operation; Helling’s objective future-health inquiry remains effective from 1993-06-18.

**Holdings navigation:** Helling v. McKinney, 509 U.S. 25 (1993); Actual awareness and unreasonable disregard of substantial danger; Circumstantial proof and reconsideration of summary judgment; Current danger governs preventive relief.

## Standards and Tests selection: Anonymous individual political leaflets

### Anonymous individual political leaflets

**Governing question:** Compelled identification on an individual’s independently produced political issue leaflets.

**Current rule:** A content-defined demand that an individual identify herself on ordinary political issue leaflets burdens core political speech, including anonymity, and requires exacting scrutiny: narrow tailoring to an overriding state interest. Viewpoint neutrality or the election setting does not lower scrutiny. General source-evaluation interests do not justify a name-and-residence-or-business-address mandate on truthful independent individual leaflets; fraud prevention requires a narrowly fitted connection rather than categorical identification of such advocacy.

**Authority by component:**

- Compelled identification on these political leaflets requires exacting scrutiny: Compelled identification on these political leaflets requires exacting scrutiny, 1995-04-19. Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer: seven direct rationale votes. Justice Thomas concurs only in the judgment on his distinct anonymous-political-pamphlet ground; Justice Scalia dissents.
- The asserted voter-information interest does not justify this identification demand: The asserted voter-information interest does not justify this identification demand, 1995-04-19. Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer: seven direct rationale votes. Justice Thomas concurs only in the judgment on his distinct anonymous-political-pamphlet ground; Justice Scalia dissents.
- Fraud prevention does not justify this application to truthful independent advocacy: Fraud prevention does not justify this application to truthful independent advocacy, 1995-04-19. Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer: seven direct rationale votes. Justice Thomas concurs only in the judgment on his distinct anonymous-political-pamphlet ground; Justice Scalia dissents.

**Present operation effective:** 1995-04-19; the component authorities identified above.

**Open question:** Candidate finance, committees, coordinated expenditures, large contributions and organizational spending remain distinct. Fraud, impersonation and appropriately tailored disclosure restrictions remain regulable. No universal personal-correspondence or small-item exemption is created.

**Holdings navigation:** Compelled identification on these political leaflets requires exacting scrutiny; The asserted voter-information interest does not justify this identification demand; Fraud prevention does not justify this application to truthful independent advocacy.

## Standards and Tests selection: Election-finance reporting, sponsor identification and political-request records

### Election-finance reporting, sponsor identification and political-request records

**Governing question:** What justification and operative conditions govern election-finance reports, on-message sponsor identification and public political-request records?

**Current rule:** **Ordinary electioneering-finance reports:** Government must establish a material connection between the information demanded and a legitimate electoral-information or source-tracing interest. A claimant seeking protective relief must substantiate the asserted associational injury; government retains justification of remaining exposure. Direct production or airing costs aggregating more than $10,000 in a calendar year trigger a report within 24 hours of each disclosure date and each later additional over-$10,000 aggregate. The report identifies the disburser, activity directors/controllers, records custodian and nonindividual principal place of business; disbursements over $200 and recipients; and relevant elections and candidates known or to be identified. Donors of $1,000 or more are identified over the period from the first day of the preceding calendar year through disclosure.

When the communication is paid from the qualifying segregated account consisting solely of direct contributions for electioneering communications by individual citizens, nationals or lawful permanent residents, donor disclosure is confined to that account, which may also be used for other purposes. Otherwise the statute reaches qualifying contributors to the disburser, not merely earmarked advertising donors. Reporting supplements other duties and preserves tax-law definitions. A demonstrated reasonable probability of threats, harassment or reprisals supports protective relief; disproportionate concrete associational burdens remain reviewable.

**Authority by component:** [McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, December 10, 2003 — Ordinary electioneering-finance reports](../terms/OT2003/records/mcconnell_v_federal_election_commission_merits_2003-12-10.md#holdings). Stone-Zsela's portion of the Court's opinion; direct joins by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, including the author (9 Justices), controlling at the exact scope stated.

**Executed contracts under section 304(f)(5):** An executed binding purchase obligation may be treated as a reportable disbursement before payment. Under the effective rule public distribution triggers the initial report after the aggregate threshold is exceeded; that report may include executed obligations for other communications that have not yet aired. The duty concerns actual financial commitments, with the same statutory thresholds, government-borne material-information connection and supported associational protections, rather than negotiations or preliminary drafts. All nine agree that unpaid obligations for an already disseminated communication are reportable.

**Authority by component:** [McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, December 10, 2003 — Executed contracts under section 304(f)(5)](../terms/OT2003/records/mcconnell_v_federal_election_commission_merits_2003-12-10.md#holdings). Stone-Zsela's portion of the Court's opinion; direct joins by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer, including the author (6 Justices), controlling at the exact scope stated. All nine join reporting unpaid obligations for an already disseminated communication. Only the six named sustaining Justices approve reporting executed contracts for separate unbroadcast communications.

**The section 212 advance-reporting challenge:** Government must justify the material electoral-information or source-tracing connection, with supported associational relief and justification of remaining exposure as stated for section 201. Statutory reports are due within 24 hours for $1,000-or-more independent-expenditure aggregates after the twentieth day but more than 24 hours before election, and within 48 hours for $10,000-or-more aggregates up to and including the twentieth day, with reports for successive corresponding aggregates for the same election. Contracts are included; receipt constitutes filing for the $1,000 report. The effective rule measures the deadlines from public distribution or dissemination.

**Authority by component:** [McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, December 10, 2003 — The section 212 advance-reporting challenge](../terms/OT2003/records/mcconnell_v_federal_election_commission_merits_2003-12-10.md#holdings). Stone-Zsela's portion of the Court's opinion; direct joins by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer, including the author (6 Justices), controlling at the exact scope stated.

**Sponsor identification: section 311:** Section 311's challenged extension of sponsor identification to electioneering communications and other covered non-express advocacy is sustained. Government must justify the material electoral-information or source-tracing connection; a claimant must substantiate protective injury while government retains justification of remaining exposure. Factual designation of the responsible sponsor has that relation to the covered paid communication and is distinct from compelled ideological endorsement. This on-message duty has its own scope and does not acquire section 201's $10,000 reporting threshold.

**Authority by component:** [McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, December 10, 2003 — Sponsor identification: section 311](../terms/OT2003/records/mcconnell_v_federal_election_commission_merits_2003-12-10.md#holdings). Stone-Zsela's portion of the Court's opinion; direct joins by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer, including the author (8 Justices), controlling at the exact scope stated.

**Broadcaster records of political requests: section 504:** Government must justify the information's material electoral or broadcast-accountability connection; supported concrete protective injury and justification of remaining exposure remain material. Licensees must maintain for public inspection records of accepted and rejected requests to buy broadcast time by or for a legally qualified candidate for public office, or for a message about a political matter of national importance, including a legally qualified candidate, a federal election or a national legislative issue of public importance. Required fields include acceptance/rejection, charged rate, airing date/time, time class and pertinent candidate/office, election or issue. Candidate requests identify the candidate, authorized committee and treasurer; other requests identify purchaser, contact name/address/telephone and chief executive officers or executive-committee/board members. Information must be placed in the file as soon as possible and retained for at least two years.

**Authority by component:** [McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, December 10, 2003 — Broadcaster records of political requests: section 504](../terms/OT2003/records/mcconnell_v_federal_election_commission_merits_2003-12-10.md#holdings). Stone-Zsela's portion of the Court's opinion; direct joins by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer, including the author (6 Justices), controlling at the exact scope stated. Thomas additionally joins the candidate-request branch, including refusals, and aired noncandidate federal-candidate/election records, making seven for those applications. The six named Justices join the other applications and the complete reversal.

**Authority by component:** [McConnell v. Federal Election Commission, December 10, 2003, reporting, contract, sponsorship and political-request components, with each coalition identified above](../terms/OT2003/records/mcconnell_v_federal_election_commission_merits_2003-12-10.md#holdings).

**Present operation effective:** December 10, 2003.

**Exceptions and limits:** Each duty retains its own trigger and threshold. The on-message identification duty does not acquire section 201’s monetary threshold, political-request files include the supported unaired-request class, and negotiations or preliminary drafts are not executed obligations. Government retains justification of remaining exposure after a supported protective claim; no unestablished confidentiality procedure is assumed.

**Related current rules:** “Issue advocacy and definite campaign-finance coverage” supplies the actual electioneering definition and its exclusions. Reporting and sponsor identification retain the independent information-duty justification, triggers and protective-relief requirements stated here; statutory speech coverage does not by itself authorize suppression.

## Standards and Tests selection: Cigarette-labeling preemption by statutory period and predicate duty

### Cigarette-labeling preemption by statutory period and predicate duty

**Governing question:** Preemption of cigarette warning duties and smoking-health advertising restrictions under the 1965 and amended 1969 provisions.

**Current rule:** Original §5 of the 1965 Act bars positive enactments requiring particular cautionary statements on cigarette packages or in advertising; it does not displace the presented common-law damages claims. Federal warning compliance does not itself confer immunity.

For federally compliant packages, amended §5(b) reaches common-law duties imposing additional or clearer smoking-health warnings in advertising or promotion, including liability premised on advertising's neutralization of the mandated warning. Identify the duty necessary for liability rather than its pleading label. The clause preserves: voluntarily undertaken express warranties, because the manufacturer supplies their substantive promise; claims resting solely on testing, research or other nonpromotional conduct or an independently actionable nonpromotional disclosure duty; and general intentional material falsehood, including advertising falsehood, when liability does not prescribe additional warning content or punish warning neutralization. A conspiracy claim survives only insofar as its predicate deceptive duty survives. Advertising as evidence does not necessarily make the underlying duty promotional, but assigning consumer warnings to an alternative channel does not by itself establish an independent duty.

For cigarettes with federally compliant packages, 15 U.S.C. section 1334(b) also reaches a State's smoking-and-health prohibition on advertising or promotion by location. A placement prohibition remains a requirement or prohibition with respect to cigarette advertising; a child-protection aim does not remove its smoking-and-health basis. The clause is not confined to additional warning text. General zoning unconnected to smoking and health and independent restrictions on sales to minors remain outside this holding. Smokeless tobacco and cigars are not directly covered by this cigarette clause.

**Authority by component:**

- Original-Act construction: Cipollone v. Liggett Group, Inc., “The 1965 Act does not displace these common-law damages claims”, June 24, 1992; Stevens, Stone, White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Kennedy and Souter.
- Covered warning and neutralization duties under the successor clause: *Cipollone*, “The successor clause reaches covered warning and warning-neutralization duties”; Stevens, Stone, White and O'Connor plus Scalia and Thomas expressly support that operative proposition.
- Warranty, independent nonpromotional duties, intentional falsehood and surviving conspiracy: *Cipollone*, “Voluntarily undertaken express warranties survive,” “Independently actionable nonpromotional conduct remains outside the clause,” and “General intentional falsehood and surviving concealment conspiracies are not barred.” The record identifies Stevens's four-member narrower grounds as controlling under Marks, with Blackmun, Kennedy and Souter's broader no-common-law-preemption grounds; each surviving category is a logical subset producing the same result, with seven judgment supporters. No whole amended-Act opinion or blanket common-law exemption is adopted.

- Smoking-health advertising-location prohibitions and surviving boundaries: Canonical Decision Record `Lorillard_Tobacco_Co_v_Reilly_merits_2001-06-28.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. Covered cigarette advertising is expressly preempted, 2001-06-28; five direct joins.

**Present operation effective:** Lorillard, June 28, 2001, for advertising-location prohibitions; Cipollone, June 24, 1992, retains each statutory-period and common-law-duty construction.

**Exceptions and limits:** Preserved claims still require an actual state-law duty and all applicable elements. No agency-disclosure duty, design-defect ruling, later-amendment construction, cigarette field immunity or generic bar on independently established actual-conflict preemption is supplied. Gade's negative overlap rule and Morales's separate airline language retain their own scopes.

**Holdings navigation:** [Lorillard Tobacco Co. v. Reilly; Altadis U.S.A. Inc. v. Reilly — Federal preemption of cigarette advertising restrictions](HOLDINGS.md#lorillard-tobacco-co-v-reilly-altadis-usa-inc-v-reilly).

## Standards and Tests selection: Discriminatory routing, charges and linked subsidies in interstate commerce

### Discriminatory routing, charges and linked subsidies in interstate commerce

**Governing question:** When a state or local economic measure must satisfy the discrimination rule rather than ordinary incidental-burden balancing.

**Current rule:** A measure discriminates when it favors local economic interests by burdening interstate competitors, including a waste charge expressly keyed to out-of-state origin, compulsory routing that reserves a processing service to a designated local private operator, or an integrated assessment-and-distribution scheme that collects from the whole market but returns the proceeds only to local producers. The entire linked operation matters; formally equal collection does not cleanse its discriminatory distribution. The government must show a legitimate local purpose that cannot adequately be served by reasonable nondiscriminatory alternatives. Ordinary incidental-burden balancing does not validate discrimination. Conservation, sanitation, cost recovery and financing a favored private facility do not themselves meet that burden; contracting with a private operator does not make compulsory market regulation governmental market participation. A municipality that actually purchases collection and disposal may specify the destination as part of that purchased performance, including through a paid hauler and privately owned facility. Separate suppliers or prices do not themselves turn purchased disposal into unrelated downstream business. This bounded purchasing authority does not reach independent transactions merely because government has a contract or financial stake. In comparing regulated distribution businesses with independent commodity sellers, actual compulsory rate, reliability and public-service obligations may distinguish the offerings. Commodity overlap alone does not establish equivalence where a separate sales category free of those obligations has not been shown. Neither a utility label nor equal taxation of local outsiders suffices by itself; no utility immunity or new public-service exception to established discrimination follows. Public ownership of a disposal facility alone does not establish governmental purchase of independent generators’ or haulers’ transactions compelled by routing or burdened by a fee. A claimed public-service distinction must therefore be assessed separately from the purchased-performance protection.

Routing locally generated waste to a genuinely public facility does not facially discriminate against interstate commerce when local private processors and out-of-state processors are treated alike. Whether the facility is genuinely public turns on its actual ownership, control, financing, public-service responsibility and revenues, and the absence of concealed private favoritism; public title alone does not settle the question.

A diversion fee survives only insofar as its actual incidence and amount are genuinely tied to diversion-related costs rather than interstate origin or protection of local commerce. A permissible public routing distinction does not establish that connection.

**Authority by component:**

- Origin-based surcharge and justification burden: Oregon Waste Systems, Inc. v. Department of Environmental Quality — An express waste-origin surcharge triggers the discrimination rule; Conservation and cost-recovery labels do not justify this private-facility differential, 1994-04-04. Thomas's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg; eight Justices directly adopt this proposition and its application.
- Private processing monopoly and neutral alternatives: C & A Carbone, Inc. v. Town of Clarkstown — Compulsory use of this local private processor discriminates in the service market; Sanitary service and financing do not justify this discriminatory route, 1994-05-16. Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Thomas and Ginsburg; six Justices adopt the discrimination classification and its stated private-service boundary. O'Connor agrees only with the judgment on a distinct Pike ground. Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Thomas and Ginsburg; six Justices adopt this application of the discrimination rule. No independent Pike holding is adopted by that coalition.
- Integrated levy, local distribution and justification: West Lynn Creamery, Inc. v. Healy — The assessment and dedicated local distribution must be examined together; the local preference lacks a sufficient justification, 1994-06-17. Justice Stevens's opinion, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg: six Justices adopt this rule and its application. Justices Scalia and Thomas concur in the judgment on the narrower dedicated-industry-tax ground. Justice Stevens's opinion, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg: six Justices adopt the justification analysis and its application. Eight Justices support reversal and remand; Justice Blackmun dissents.
- SSC — Part I, genuine purchased-performance boundary, 1996-03-11; Kennedy for all nine; Part II applies Carbone to the separate compulsory ordinance without changing its test. 
- Bounded regulated-service comparison: General Motors v. Tracy — General Motors Corp. v. Tracy — II. This record does not establish the asserted discrimination, February 18, 1997; Souter, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. The Court does not reach compensatory-tax justification or independent Pike balancing.

- Holdings 1–3: Stone-Zsela’s Opinion of the Court, joined in full by O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, five direct votes: Waste Management, Inc. of Tennessee v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County — controlling Holdings, 1998-05-27.

**Present operation effective:** SSC, March 11, 1996, for the affirmative purchased-performance boundary; the existing discrimination test remains unchanged. Waste Management, May 27, 1998, for the public-facility classification and independent diversion-cost requirement.

**Exceptions and limits:** These decisions do not adjudicate every general-revenue subsidy, genuinely public waste system or government-owned landfill. The public-facility rule supplies no blanket immunity. A compensatory tax must independently satisfy the requirements in “Compensatory taxes and the actual equivalent local burden.”

**Holdings navigation:** An express waste-origin surcharge triggers the discrimination rule; Conservation and cost-recovery labels do not justify this private-facility differential; Compulsory use of this local private processor discriminates in the service market; Sanitary service and financing do not justify this discriminatory route; The assessment and dedicated local distribution must be examined together; The local preference lacks a sufficient justification; SSC Corp. v. Town of Smithtown, judgment below 66 F.3d 502. General Motors Corp. v. Tracy (1997-02-18) — This record does not establish the asserted discrimination. Waste Management, Inc. of Tennessee v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County — Public waste routing and separate diversion charges.



**Current wording authority:** Tracy, February 18, 1997, clarifies the practical comparator at the stated service/record boundary; it does not change the existing discrimination, compensation or conditional-remedy rules.
